speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING GOVERNMENT MARKETING AND PRICE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire at this time to make a brief statement in connection with some aspects of the 1944-45 grain policy.
The house will recall that last September a major change was made in wheat policy and a basis was established, effective until July 31, 1945, which of course includes the full crop year 1944-45. At that time the fixed initial price of wheat was increased to $1.25 per bushel for No. 1 northern wheat in store, Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. This fixed initial price will be in effect for the coming crop year.
In regard to the wheat policy for 1944-45, the government has yet to determine the quantity of wheat which will be marketable in that crop year. Members will recall that for
1943-	44 the limitation was first placed at fourteen bushels per authorized acre and was later increased to eighteen bushels per authorized acre-the understanding being that about 280,000,000 bushels of wheat would be marketable in western Canada during the present crop year.
The government is not prepared at the moment to state the exact quantity of wheat which will be marketable in the coming crop year, owing to the uncertainties of the growing crop and uncertainty in respect to the volume of transportation which will be available for the movement of grains in 1944-45. In establishing the basis of marketings for the coming crop year, which will be announced at a later date, the government will take into account probable domestic and export demand in
1944-	45 as well as the volume of grain which the railroads and elevators can handle during the crop year.
I can say at this time that the demand for grain both in Canada and for export is now running at veTy high levels and that the volume of wheat which will be marketable in 1944-45 will be considerably larger than the limitation in effect during the past two crop years.
I might refer briefly to the present grain position. Accumulated stocks of wheat are

moving rapidly into consumption here and abroad and the main problem to-day is meeting demand with the transportation which is available for the movement of grain. It is estimated that the carry-over of wheat next July will amount to about 330,000,000 bushels as compared to over 600,000,000 bushels last July. Given adequate transportation the crop year 1944-45 will see our wheat stocks reduced to a nominal figure. Oats and barley are in good demand and there will be no difficulty in disposing of surpluses from the 1944 crop. The expansion in the acreage seeded to these grains in recent years has been more than justified by marketings and the Department of Agriculture is urging that seeding of at least as great an acreage as in 1944.
The government's policy in regard to oats and barley for 1944-45 will be the same as in 1943-44. Minimum prices for these grains will be. guaranteed on the same basis as in 1943-44. Equalization funds will again operate and the government will make advance payments free from the equalization funds at the time of delivery. The advance payments are ten cenits per bushel for oats and fifteen cents per bushel for barley.
The government has already announced that there will be a guaranteed price for flax of $2.75 per bushel for No. 1 CW flax, basis in store Fort William and Port Arthur or Vancouver. This represents an increase of twenty-five cents per bushel over the guaranteed price in effect in 1943-44.
Respecting sunflower seed and rape seed the government's policy for the 1944-45 crop year is to continue in effect the prices for these seeds established for the 1943^44 season. That is to say, the Canadian wheat board will be authorized to pay five cents per pound for sunflower seed and six cents per pound for rape seed, delivered f.o.b. shipping points to be designated by the board for the top grades.

1.	Did the government receive a deputation of the mayor, controllers and aldermen of Toronto this week regarding the housing situation?
2.	What action will be taken to provide houses in Toronto for, (a) soldiers' families; (b) civilians?
3.	What reply was given to the deputation, And will any action on their request be announced, and when?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2 and 3. The following letter signed by the Minister of Finance was sent to the mayor of Toronto:
"The city clerk's letter of April 19, 1944, transmitting the text of a resolution of the Toronto board of control, as well as the supplementary representations made to me and to my colleague, Mr. Howe, have been, carefully considered.
I must advise you that the government has come to the conclusion that no change can be made in the policy announced nearly a month ago and reiterated on several recent occasions. As indicated in the previous statements referred to, the government feels that the wartime prices and trade board has gone to the limit in imposing restrictions on the ordinary rights of an owner to obtain possession of his property.
Dealing with the specific proposal contained in the resolution adopted by the board of control, this proposal would place upon the wartime prices and trade board a responsibility which it should not assume and which it is not equipped to discharge.
Moreover, I question whether any county court judge should be asked to decide as to the respective needs of landlord and tenant in particular instances, and I would fear that the enactment of an order in council such as has been suggested would result in the courts being overburdened with applications by tenants-some good, some bad-which it would be quite impossible to dispose of within the period contemplated in the resolution.
As to the other recommendations contained [DOT]in the resolution concerning the provision of low-cost housing, while this does not affect the immediate problem of possible evictions on May 1, these recommendations are being given most careful consideration."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have before me a questionnaire in reference to which I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. This questionnaire is being circulated to-day among the various home defence units by officers apparently authorized by National Defence headquarters. In the questionnaire the various personnel are asked whether they will sign active, whether their family has been affected adversely or advantageously by the war, whether a civil job is held open for them

Army-Home Defence
after the war, whether they would consider signing active if service guaranteed under French-speaking officers and N.C.O.'s, and whether they have any other reason for not signing active. The questions I desire to ask arise in connection with that questionnaire and also in connection with the statement made the other day by General Pearkes, Y.C. Have instructions gone forth from National Defence headquarters that officers of the various units are to interview their personnel with a view to inducing or coercing them to enlist for overseas service? Have instructions been given to these officers to advise the men that unless fifty per cent of them are secured for active service, conscription for overseas service will be put into effect, and generally what is the situation with respect to reinforcements for the army overseas? These are matters which I think are urgent, having regard to recent statements that have been made.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: QUESTIONNAIRE TO HOME DEFENCE TROOPS AS TO ATTESTATION FOR OVERSEAS SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take the usual course and ask for time in which to answer the question asked by my hon. friend. This is the first I have heard of the questionnaire to which he refers. I have nothing to say with regard to the questionnaire; I presume it is being circulated by officers who desire to get that information, which I am sure would be very useful to the Department of National Defence.
The hon. member asks whether any instructions have gone forward for officers to interview personnel in the units with a view to inducing them or "coercing" them-I think that was the word he used-to enlist for overseas service, or with a view to threatening that if more than fifty per cent did not enlist for overseas service, conscription would be introduced. I want to say to my hon. friend and to the house that two or three weeks ago a meeting was held of the officers commanding the different districts for the purpose of discussing the matter of recruiting. The house knows, I presume-I have indicated this to the house previously-the sources from which overseas personnel come. They are the general service personnel in the units in Canada; the N.R.M.A. personnel in the units who may volunteer for general service; the general service personnel in the training centres, and those who are recruited from time to time. It was thought highly advisable that the army should do its duty with regard to the raising and maintaining of the volunteer army overseas of which Canada is exceedingly proud; and I have not heard anyone in this house or anywhere else suggest that 100-150
the volunteer army was not a desirable thing. I have indicated repeatedly that I prefer a voluntary army, and I think most Canadians will agree with me. In that connection the army has its duty to maintain, if it can, that volunteer army; and for that purpose the army has engaged in recruiting activities for the last three years. The activities which are referred to or which are implied in the questionnaire to which my hon. friend has referred I presume are the result of the conferences which have been held. No such questionnaire was authorized in express terms, but I do not repudiate it, nor do I see anything whatever wrong in it. The same sort of questionnaire might well be circulated to anyone who was being asked to subscribe for victory bonds. Persuasion is being used in Canada at the present time by way of meetings, by bringing very prominent people here, by way generally of persuading people to subscribe their money for a good three per cent security. It seems to me that the army is not only entitled to see to it, but it is the duty of the army to see to it, that the needs of the volunteer army are put before the people of Canada in exactly the same way. That is being done and will be done; and when my hon. friend uses the word "coerce" he uses a word which is not only unauthorized but is totally unjustified in any shape or form.

speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: QUESTIONNAIRE TO HOME DEFENCE TROOPS AS TO ATTESTATION FOR OVERSEAS SERVICE
speechtext: There is plenty of coercion.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: QUESTIONNAIRE TO HOME DEFENCE TROOPS AS TO ATTESTATION FOR OVERSEAS SERVICE
speechtext:
I want to say to my hon. friend that I know of no coercion. I do not desire to cast any reflection at all upon the war loan campaign, but I say to my hon. friend that I do not think any inducement or any effort is being put forward in connection with recruiting that is comparable to the effort being put forward by citizens of this country to endeavour to induce and persuade their fellow citizens to subscribe their money. I make no apology whatever for asking men to enlist in the service, and I deprecate more than I can say the attempt which has been made to disparage recruiting activities in Canada. There has been a constant effort to do that. Only the other day the suggestion was made that because a great soldier went out west and addressed the soldiers there, indicating what the needs of the army were and what had been his experiences overseas, he was being humiliated. No such suggestion is made when great people come here and tell us of the need for money, and try to influence us to buy bonds. That is regarded as in every way desirable; we attend these meetings and

Army-Home Defence

rallies. But recruiting seems to be something which must be disparaged, and I can only think it must be because there is some sort of fetish on the part of some people for conscription. The objective is not to get men for the army; the objective is to get men, provided you get them by conscription; and I want to say that with these people it seems to be the method rather than the result which is important.
The army proposes to keep right straight on in connection with its recruiting activities. Right here and now I want to thank the citizens of this country who have helped so valiantly in connection with recruiting all over Canada, and I am going to ask those citizens to keep on, and not to be disconcerted in any way by the efforts which are being made in some quarters to suggest that recruiting activity is something in which it is unworthy to engage. That is all I have to say in answer to my hon. friend's question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the hon. the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). Is an investigation now being held on the terrible accident that occurred in Montreal on Tuesday last, when a bomber crashed in the heart of the city, and will the government take action with a view to compensating the people who have suffered damage?
Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National
Defence for Air) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I have had no notice of that question, but I have seen in the papers, this morning, that the Montreal coroner has just opened an investigation on that accident.. In the second place, an investigation is also being held by the R.A.F. in Montreal, at the headquarters of Aviation District No. 3; it is presided over by an officer of the R.A.F. and Aviation Inspector Blondeau, of the Department of Transport, and Squadron Leader Gobeil, of the R.C.A.F., are attending it. We are now considering whether those two investigations will be sufficient to satisfy the public and the government. If we find, as a result of an inquiry which is now under way, that it would be desirable to pursue an investigation more extensive than those that are now going on, the government will take a decision and inform the house.

The interview referred to was hardly a press interview. It was simply a question as to the accuracy of a newspaper article. In time it was found that supplies in hand were adequate for that particular time and about two thirds of the capacity was closed. The tempp of the war is

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, April 24, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette. in the chair.

War Appropriation-War Services
Corps of (civilian) Canadian fire fighters for United Kingdom, $744,905.

This question of firemen
from Canada in the United Kingdom was up last year about a month after the minister took charge of the department-I think it was July. At that time the minister said he was going to look into it and make some changes, owing to the fact that the civilian fire fighters of England were assuming their regular duties and that the raids were few and far between. I appreciate what the firemen have done. I have some letters here from firemen who served overseas. I shall send them to the minister. One of them is from a fireman living at Billings avenue in Toronto in the constituency of the hon. member for Greenwood. This fireman has just returned from England. He points out that there is really nothing for them to do there. Efe says they are doing nothing in the line of fire duty as the regular fire services in England are looking after all the little bombings that are going on. The corps of Canadians in Southampton and Bristol have never been in a raid, according to this fireman. He never saw one while he was there, and he was there for two years. He says on March 10, 1943, he moved to Portsmouth and they had one small raid on August 16 of that year. He says that the group at Plymouth have had a little action. They are looking after their own camps and fields in England. He refers me to the fire chiefs of two large cities of Canada, one in western Ontario and the other in Halifax. He refers also to two officers in the Toronto fire department. He is asking for further information.
I appreciate what the minister has done in reducing the item. It has been reduced from $957,850 to $744,905. Are these firemen overseas working actively? There are practically no raids. The raids have been eliminated. Firemen may have been necessary in the first and second years of the war during the battles of London, Coventry and Cardiff. But because of the waj the raids have been reduced surely we do not need three-quarters of a million dollars in the estimates to cover this item when some of the firemen have returned home. When fire departments in the mother country are going back to their civil occupations, why should we have a large staff over there, when men are needed in Canada and in the forces overseas? After all is said and done we must not forget that wars are won by soldiers, sailors and airmen at the scene of combat. The same applies to firemen; they must work at the scenes of fires. That is where they are needed. They are not needed
at home when men are required in the army. Dear knows where we will be when the time for invasion comes.
As I have said, the time has come when we should give some consideration to the municipalities. Sitting here as a committee we should reduce the item by two-thirds. I be-believe good work was done over there by a splendid body of men. They learned a great deal about fighting fires. We know there was a time when Canada might have been invaded, because the enemy was pretty close to our shores.	[DOT]
In passing may I compliment the minister. I had much to do with him during the last war and I found him always to be an obliging official. Last session when we were talking about salvage he said he would look into the matter, with the intention of possibly reducing it.
The question now arises as to whether those men are or are not needed over there.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): I would remind the committee that a request for Canadian firefighters was made by the British government, and they were sent by the Canadian government in response to that request. At that time there was no question of our troops leaving the British isles. In those days the British isles were strictly on the defensive, and behind those defences preparations were being made to do what we hope may soon be done successfully. Up to now there have been tens of thousands of people in the national fire service devoting their time to preparing defences against enemy raids, and particularly defences against incendiaries. Our very brave fire fighters, each a volunteer, have been stationed in dangerous centres. They have been in raids-thank heaven only a very few have suffered from the effects of enemy bombing. But they stand on duty over there, and do suffer the monotonies connected therewith. We know that wherever we find a group of men who are not actively engaged against the enemy each day, or almost each day, they suffer from monotony. But so do the firemen in fire halls who stand by to save our dwellings and business places here at home.
May I point out that there has been a reduction of $212,945 in the vote. It is necessary to make provision for all the services, pay and allowances, lodgings, travelling expenses and everything else for that body of men, not knowing how long it will be necessary to keep the corps in the British isles. It was seriously considered during the early part of last winter whether the corps would be left in

War Appropriation-War Services
England. After taking the best possible advice, including the considered opinions of British fire fighting authorities and the British government, it was decided to leave them there. I believe those in England who gave us the benefit of their advice, knowledge and recommendations anticipated what we believe will take place shortly, when our army moves against the enemy, let us say on the continent of Europe.
We have had an intimation that possibly the imperial force, the national fire service of Great Britain, will offer an opportunity to some of the members of our corps to join them in certain extra duties which possibly would take them beyond the British isles. That matter is receiving attention to-day. No decision has been taken, because we have not all the information. I bring the matter to the attention of the committee because, there again, it may be that Canada will go along in the vanguard of the invading forces, in the defence of all we hold dear.
If the war ends quickly the corps will be brought back as 'quickly as possible. If the raids over Great Britain continue it will be extremely difficult indeed to bring them back until we have reached safety. That is the situation in regard to the corps overseas. I have had the very best reports about them- their lodgings, their meals, their equipment, and their clothing. I am extremely happy to say that upon reading the reports which come to us, the conduct and discipline indicated therein show that members of , the corps honour it, by their very good conduct, and thereby have gained esteem in the eyes of their neighbours in Great Britain. Hardly an offence worth mentioning has been lodged against any member of the corps.
May I repeat that I sympathize with men who must sit and wait until the enemy comes over to bomb them.

Have there been no definite transfers of men who went over with the corps? A letter which came to me yesterday indicates that transfers have been made. One man, I know, became tired of the monotonous life and, upon application, was transferred.
Mr. LaFLECHE: A small number have volunteered for Canada's fighting forces, and several have gone with the auxiliary services.

How many are there remaining in Great Britain?
Mr. LaFLECHE: There are 362.

How many went over?

Mr. LaFLECHE: In all, 417 were recruited. Only one is deceased, and his death was due to an accident over there. His widow is pensioned.	'

Where is the reduction in the amount? I must say I disagree sharply with the hon. member for Broadview. I receive numerous letters from London, the west of England and some from Yorkshire, and I know from recent letters that bombings in the last couple of months have been pretty bad. Many thousands of incendiaries have been dropped on some of the larger centres mentioned by the hon. member. I was just wondering what were the reasons for this reduction. I agree with the minister who said that while many of these men must of necessity be posted at points where conditions are monotonous, you cannot tell where a bomb is going to fall. At any moment they may be invaluable to the local community. Those of us who have visited the old country know that there are places which are under almost constant bombing. The hon. member for Parry Sound is in his place and he will remember that we visited one city which is seldom mentioned as having been bombed to any extent but which in fact was one of the worst-bombed places that we saw. Before I approve what the hon. member for Broadview has suggested, that this vote be reduced by two-thirds, I would want to be assured that there is a good and valid reason for any reduction that has been made already.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I shall compare the items in this vote with the vote of last year, and then I shall have another word to say about the necessity of keeping the corps together until we know more about the results of what lies ahead. There is a very definite connection between the two.
The items are:
	This year	Last year
Salaries 	$ 2,220	$ 2.850Pay	370,000	395,000Subsistence allowance	116,330	250,000Dependents' allowance....	150,000	172,000Clothing and equipment..	65.000	100,000Medical care and hos-	pitalization 	, 9,500	9,500Transportation 	25,500	15,000Printing and stationery. .	1,000	3,000Miscellaneous 	5,000	10,000Cost of living bonus	325	430Unemployment insurance..	30	70
The reduction in the pay item is brought about by the reduction in the force. Last year we provided for 400 men, and this year we are providing for 362 men, all ranks. The pay item of $370,000 is worked out by the financial officers. They know how many men of all ranks they must provide for, for 365
23S9

War Appropriation-TVar Services
days. This is the figure. The subsistence allowance is calculated for the full year and is in accordance with the number of persons to be provided for. This covers the cost of food and lodging. I have it on the best authority that these men have an excellent table. They are provided with the regular rations which can be improved with proper care and preparation. They are lodged in very comfortable buildings and they have upon them the benevolent eye of their fellow firemen in the national fire service. .
Some items of equipment were issued when the corps was set up and they need not be renewed, but clothing must be renewed regularly. Up to date we have authorized, as it became necessary in the eyes of the commanding and other responsible officers of the corps overseas, two and one half issues of clothing. The original clothing was purchased in Canada because the men were here. At a moderate cost each member of the corps was provided with a semi-fitting uniform which was then fitted to him by competent tailors. The same practice is being followed in England, and this corps is able to present an extremely smart appearance without its costing more than it should. The amount of $65,000 is considered sufficient to provide the necessary new shoes and clothing and equipment to the members of the corps.
The increase of $10,500 in the item for transportation reflects to some extent the possibility of bringing back to Canada a number of these men, buit, as I have explained already, circumstances which have been inquired into very carefully tell us that they should remain there because they are badly needed. These are gallant men and I am certain they do not want to come home until they have done their full job.

I did not catch the reduction in personnel overseas which the minister gave.
Mr. LaFLECHE: There has been a reduction of 38.

How did that occur?
Were men returned to Canada or transferred to other services? I know that one man died.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The reduction in personnel has been quite gradual. Casualties are always to be expected for one reason or another. All the reasons mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar can be offered for the reduction. Unfortunately one man was killed. The physical condition of others has deteriorated overseas, but this occurs in all groups of men.

Some have been brought home?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes.

How many?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Since the beginning there have been discharged or struck off strength a total of 60 men. Twelve were discharged in Canada before the corps proceeded overseas; one died overseas; ten were discharged overseas in order to join active or auxiliary services, and thirty-seven were returned to Canada for discharge.

Mr. Chairman, after the blitz in London, there was a campaign in Canada to send firemen's ladders to Great Britain. While that campaign was on, a firemen's convention was held in a United States city, which the fire chief of a Canadian city attended, and there he had a talk with the fire chief of that United States city and spoke about this campaign for ladders to be shipped to Britain. To his great surprise he learned that that very city had called for tenders for new firemen's ladders and that the lowest tender had come from Great Britain. That showed that the British people were not so much excited over the blitz that they were forgetting trade. They were asking us to ship them ladders and at the same time were offering to sell ladders at the cheapest price to that city in the United States. That I think is a lesson for all of us that we should not forget during the war.

I
listened to the hon. member for Broadview and I cannot find myself in accord with him. He stated that the bombing of Britain had ceased. I think probably, Mr. Chairman, we are taking too much for granted. The bombings may have ceased for the time being, but I do not think we should take for granted that the bombings have permanently ceased. Too often in Canada we are apt to feel that the war is getting away from us, too far away. I feel that we are very much in this war, just as much to-day as ever we were, and we are still a long way from winning it. It is possible that there may still be very heavy bombings of Great Britain.
I was glad the other day, Mr. Chairman, to hear the minister say that he hoped that the members of this fire fighting force would in time be entitled to the same benefits as the men who served in the armed forces. I do trust that such a regulation will soon be put into effect. These men went to Britain when there were heavy bombings and offered their lives in the protection of the persons

rrar Appropriation-TFar Services
and property of the people of that country, and they are entitled to the same benefits as the men who served in the armed forces.
There is one thing I should like to bring to [DOT]the attention of the committee as a matter of interest, and that is that when this fire fighting force was being organized the government looked over Canada for the best fire fighting chief in the country to head the force. Hon. members will be interested to know that in addition to selecting expert firemen from Brantford, the man who commanded that force, took it over to Britain and is still in command of it was the chief of the fire department of the city of Brantford.

Mr. Chairman, I have not heard anyone speak of what must have been the good effect on the morale of the people of England, if their morale could possibly have been improved, of the landing over there of firemen from Canada to assist them in putting out fires caused by bombings if they occurred. I am glad to hear that the fires did not occur to the extent that had been ahticipated, but that would not be any argument against sending the fire fighters over, because had another big blitz occurred our men would have been there to help put the fires out.
While the hon. member for Brantford City takes great credit for his city in the fact that the chief of this fire fighting force was selected from Brantford-it was an honour to his city, and I have no doubt that the chief was an expert fire fighter-I am happy to say that a very large number of the personnel of that force were recruited from Toronto. The fire fighters who went from Toronto, like those who were selected from other cities in Canada -because I am not going to claim more credit for Toronto than anywhere else-were all experienced and expert fire fighters. I have no doubt that all these selections were made because of the men's ability and experience in fighting fires. I knew quite a number of them who left Toronto to go over to Britain, and to my knowledge they were the very best men that could be sent.
Mr. LaFLECHE: My hon. friend will be interested to know that fifty-six came from Toronto.

I am proud to hear that fifty-six enlisted from Toronto. Whoever was responsible for recruiting that fire fighting force to aid the old country, which had gone through so much, deserves a great deal of credit for the formation of this force which consisted of the very cream of the fire fighters of Canada.

When the estimates of the minister were up on the last occasion, a number of questions were asked which he could not answer at the time, and he promised to bring down the information when next his estimates were up. One of the questions had to do with the possibility of men in the hospitals in Great Britain, in the Mediterranean, and in Canada, getting the benefit of these educational courses. I pointed out that my information was that the courses were not readily available to the men in hospitals, and I thought some improvement should be made in that regard. Is the minister prepared to make any statement to-day?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I should have explained before we began consideration of this item to-day that the Canadian Legion educational courses may be arranged for members of the services. But if they are not begun before the men have been discharged from the army-

They may not begin?
Mr. LaFLECHE: No, that has not yet been arranged. It is under consideration. But the courses may be completed after a man has been discharged. I have been advised that the men in hospitals overseas and here in Canada can have these courses, and it is desired that they should have them. The matter has been brought to the attention of the Department of Pensions and National Health and of the educational officers of the Canadian Legion. There was seemingly some misapprehension- but my departmental officials since we met last Monday have taken the matter up with these other authorities who are in very close contact with the men. My opinion is that these educational courses should be made available to all the men. Already nearly 200,000 members of the forces have enrolled in these courses. It may be that my hon. friend has in mind an odd case, or a few cases, perhaps in some isolated spot. But we have brought the matter to the attention of the other authorities and, as I say, I am all in favour of these courses being made available to all the men.

I think that these courses should be made available to all the men in the forces. But the minister says that a man who has been discharged from the army cannot get these courses. As the minister knows, when these men are discharged from the army and go into a pensions hospital, they become charges of the pension department, and apparently under the present regulations they cannot take a course at that time. There is great need for facilities being provided to enable the man who is in a pensions hospital

War Appropriation-War Services
to get the benefit of these educational courses. He is there wounded, or perhaps ill, and he has more time to study than he would have on active service with the navy, the army or the air force. There is great need for these courses to be provided for these men. I am told definitely by people who have visited one of the Pensions and National Health hospitals that the men are not getting the courses, certainly not to any great extent. They are very much concerned about it, and would be greatly interested in getting them. I suggest that this comes under the minister, who should see to it that the necessary arrangements are made with the Department of Pensions and National Health for the men in these big hospitals to have the full benefit of the educational courses. Has the minister taken any steps to see that this is made possible?
Mr. LaFLECHE:	I am afraid my hon.
friend did not follow me when I said that men in civilian hospitals, after being discharged from the forces, may have the courses.

You said " may not."
Mr. LaFLECHE: Just a moment; they may have the courses if they took them up before they were discharged from the army.

But that does not meet all
cases.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Just a moment, please. Then a short time ago I added that we have again taken up the matter of allowing a man to begin a course after he has been discharged and is in a Pensions and National Health hospital. I may add that to my knowledge this situation has been under discussion with the competent authorities for at least two or three months, because we want these courses given to all the boys who desire them, whether before discharge or while in hospital following discharge. We believe in these educational courses; we think they are good for the boys. Therefore we have tried-and have not found any opposition-to open up a demand for these educational courses. This educational programme began, I would remind the committee, as something for the troops while in uniform; but as the war goes on men are discharged and are kept in hospital, and these courses are good for them. So that we are doing exactly what the hon. gentleman said would be a good thing.

You are not doing it yet; you are trying to do it.
Mr. LaFLECHE: We are trying to popularize it.

What are the obstacles to getting such courses started in these hospitals? Why have they not been made available before this?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I do not know. I explained earlier when we were on this item that my department fills requisitions made upon it by the defence departments. Naturally this is for men in uniform, but men are no longer under the Department of National Defence after they have been discharged. Of our own accord we have tried to follow this into another department, and discussions are going on in order to see whether the boys will want the courses and whether the departments can make the necessary arrangements to that end. Everybody is for it.

Will that include handicraft and art courses?
Mr. LaFLECHE: They have those in the hospitals now.

Then may we take it that these educational courses will be made available to men in the Pensions and National Health hospitals within a short time?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes, most assuredly, so far as the Department of National War Services is concerned.

What about the Department of Pensions and National Health?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I cannot answer for that department, as my hon. friend knows.

But it is a government responsibility.
Mr. LaFLECHE: While a matter is under discussion between two departments it is too early to announce any decision. I have told my hon. friend very carefully what we are trying to do; now let him wait.
I do not mind waiting, but the men concerned should not be kept waiting.

I am keenly interested in the matter which has been brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver South, but without interrupting his line of thought or the minister's answers I should like to return to the matter under discussion previously, that is, the corps of civilian fire fighters overseas, in order to ask a further question. Apparently the minister is expecting these men to remain over there now. I want to associate myself with all the good things that have been said about them. Casualties of



War Appropriation-War Services
one kind or another have been suffered by some of these men, and I should like to know what is done for their families. What would be done for the family of a fire fighter overseas who became totally incapacitated, or eventually died, as the result of some injury?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am happy to be able to tell the hon. member for Lincoln that if death occurs the family is pensioned.

On the same basis as the family of a member of the overseas forces?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Under the same act. They are under the Pension Aot; that is the whole situation in a word.

Then if I may follow that up, eligibility for pension is worked out on exactly the same basis as in connection with soldiers who serve overseas?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes. If injury is suffered while on service overseas, the man is eligible for pension. As I said a moment ago the widow of one member of the corps, who was killed in an accident in Great Britain, is being pensioned.

Does the Canadian pension commission deal with these applications?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes, in precisely the same way as it deals with other applications.

I should like to say a word about these fire fighters. As I understand it, the minister is not responsible for this programme; he took it over from another minister last July. These are trained firemen whom we have sent overseas, but in many cases they are not needed there. The other day I received a letter from a fireman just back from England, in which he gave a list of the cities which said they did not need any help; they included Southampton, Bristol, Plymouth, and others. The fire fighters belonging to those cities have done the work, while, he says, the men we have sent over have not been asked to help at all. Then I should like to know where these men come from, by provinces. There is a third point. In a return brought down the other day it was stated that the loss from fire in army, navy and air force camps in Canada since the beginning of the war has amounted to about $4,500,000, with practically no insurance except what may have been taken out by a few contractors. As I said the other day, this war is a changing war; it changes from week to week, month to month and year to year, and in my opinion the need for Canadian firemen in Great Britain has practically vanished. If they should be needed there, let them stay, but in view of the letters I have received and
f Mr. Lockhart.]
the conversations I have had with some of the men who have returned, I do not believe they are needed any further in England. These men in their letters have said that they have little or nothing to do over there, and they might as well have been at home in Canada.
In this connection there is something I cannot understand at all. We have the army, the navy and the air force in Britain; they are on the job twenty-four hours a day, and they get no holidays. Right next door to them are these Canadian fire fighters, many of whom have very little to do and some of whom are given leave to come back home for a holiday. Some of the men in the forces have been over there for going on five years, but they have been given no holidays at all. The minister is a military man himself, having had a long and able career in the army, and he knows that civilian firemen receive some military drill and physical training, and he knows that under any modem fire chief there are competent instructors, so that altogether these men are hardy and quite fit for military duty. I have received, in the letter to which I referred, information that in four or five Canadian cities the chief thinks the work in England is over for these men, and I am led to believe that the men overseas, if they are kept there, should be transferred to the army. They should form as a fire unit and be a part of the army if they are to be of any use in Great Britain. I suggest that as a fire-fighting unit they should form a part of the army of invasion if we are to keep them there. We are spending three-quarters of a million on them and I fail to see the use of it. If it were necessary I would not say a word; I would go for it one hundred per cent. As matters stand, however, I do not believe it is necessary and I suggest that we should have some further explanation. The fire departments throughout Canada have suffered very considerably from a depletion of their forces. Firemen are needed in all our cities and towns because in many cases the new men are not as well equipped to fight fires as those who have had years of experience. There may be some merit in the retention of the men in their present capacity if they are to take part in a reconstruction programme in Britain, but so far we have not heard whether their duties will include the rebuilding of cities that have been bombed over there.
We wish to give the minister every encouragement in his work, and our criticism is intended to be constructive, but I suggest that this item should be cut down and as many of the men as possible drafted into the army as a fire unit. They should be transferred from the minister's department to the army. I

War Appropriation-IFar Services
understand that the civilian firemen in Great Britain are able to cope with the work they are called upon to do.
Mr. LaFLECHE: May I reassure the hon. member that if the corps is still in England it is there because the authorities there, after studying the question very carefully at our request, reported that it was necessary that they should remain there. The events of the near future may change the situation entirely, but at the moment I am quite satisfied that it is necessary that the corps should remain where they are, doing the work in which they are at present engaged until events take their course and we can see a little further into the future.

The majority will agree with the minister, I think, when he says that these fire fighters have a definite place to fill in the work in Great Britain. As he said, this request came from the British government, and so far as our information goes now that request still stands. There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister. The auditor general's report for the year ended March 31, 1943, states that each member discharged for medical unfitness or other cause, after 183 days' service, receives a clothing allowance of $35. It is my understanding that the men of the fire fighting corps have the same status as the men in the various branches of the fighting service. If that is so I cannot quite understand why the clothing allowance for these men should be as low as $35. Why is it not $65? Is this an old regulation, and has there been a change since?
Mr. LaFLECHE: The hon. member has replied to his own question. He was reading from a report made at a time when the clothing allowance in the armed forces was $35. It was raised to $65 and it has been similarly increased in the case of members of the fire fighting corps.

There is another
question. There seems to be a difference of opinion between the auditor general on the one hand and the Minister of National War Services on the other with respect to the collection of income tax from members of the corps. On page 58 of the auditor general's report the statement appears that the minister instructed the comptroller of the treasury that these taxes should not be collected from members of the force. I wish the minister would enlarge on that and say whether or not authority has been given, by way of order in 100-151i
council for example, to exempt those men who are overseas from the provisions of the income tax act.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The auditor general's report from which the hon. member is reading is presumably up to March 31, 1943, a year ago. From the very beginning there was some difficulty about income tax. There has been of course a difficulty in that regard in other cases as well. From a very early date the matter was taken up with the competent authorities of other departments and recommendations were made that the members of the corps be not subject to income tax while overseas. As yet that has not been finally decided in their favour. By arrangement at the time of the report mentioned by my hon. friend, it was decided that the paymaster should not make the deduction. At present the point is again being taken up with the competent authorities. The great difficulty is that the Canadian corps is a civilian corps, not a military one. I even thought of giving them a status which would have been a military status, but we encountered difficulties there. It was not possible to do so. That would have solved that rather small problem, but it was not possible to do that. We then went back to the other authorities and we are still discussing the merits of the recommendations I have made on more than one occasion, namely, that income tax be not applied in the case of these men once they are overseas.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
On that point may I
suggest to the minister that he look up what was done by the government in connection with the men who went to Kiska last summer. He is probably familiar with it anyway. According to the strict wording of the Income War Tax Act as amended last year, those men were taxed at the rate of fifty per cent while they were at Kiska. Following representations on the matter in the house the government decided to change the situation and did so by order in council. I suggest to the minister that he might use what was done in that case as an argument to support him in what he is trying to do for these men.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I am grateful for the . suggestion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
To follow the matter up I offer it as a suggestion.
Mr. LaFLECHE:	We are using it, but
again the position of the corps is not that of the units which went to Kiska. They were military units; the fire fighters are not. Nevertheless it is up to our department to bring it to a finality. We have to tell them finally

War Appropriation-War Services
"yes" or "no," and we are doing our very best to put the members of this corps upon the same footing in that respect as the members of the military corps.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
As a further suggestion, may I point out it seems possible to do marvellous and wonderful things by order in council. For example, the order in council to which I refer read this way, if I recall it correctly: "For income tax purposes Kiska shall be regarded as outside the western hemisphere." As the minister knows, the phrase "for purposes of" so-and-so creeps into many orders in council. It does seem to me the minister should use that argument in this way:	For income tax purposes these men
may be considered as members of the military forces.
Mr. LaFLECHE: That argument is being used, and I think I used the best argument of all, namely, that these boys who went overseas went into an area of at least as great danger as did the members of any of the armed forces. For my own satisfaction I cannot find any better argument than that. I have used it and I am going to keep on using it.

The auxiliary service groups do not get complete exemption from income tax. Why is that?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I do not know. I cannot answer for what- happens in another department. In a sense they have been given a military status and it is on that score that they receive the benefit. I attempted to attain that status for the members of the fire fighting corps but was unable to do so. Earlier this afternoon I said something about the possibility of some members of the corps being given an opportunity to go beyond the British isles presumably in the not distant future. So far as I am concerned I will not want them to go unless the matter under discussion is settled in their favour. Unfortunately if they go they will go as members of a civilian corps. I assure the committee the particular matter of military status or otherwise is the dividing point, or has been found to be the dividing point, and indeed a very high partition has been set up which we have not been able to hurdle in favour of these boys up to now.

Why is there a difference in the case of the men in the auxiliary services?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Because the others have a semi-military status.

Why do they not get complete exemption as do the men in the army?

Mr. LaFLECHE: I am not fully aware of the reason myself. They accompany the armies. I told a glorious story the other day of some supervisors of the auxiliary services putting their supplies of comforts in tanks. Those tanks were placed in ships and shipped to Sicily. The comforts were removed from the tanks and the tanks went on as fighting units. The auxiliary services took their cigarettes and chocolates and other things and went ashore for the comfort of our fighters.

I presume the civilian corps of Canadian fire fighters take their places in some organization of United Kingdom fire fighters with like duties. If that is so, is there a distinction between the military and the fire fighters in so far as income tax in Great Britain is concerned? I have an idea that may have a bearing on the point. Has the minister made any inquiries in that regard?
Mr. LaFLECHE: In England the equivalent of our fire fighters corps is known as the national fire service. That definitely is a civilian corps. I happen to know that whatever may be projected over there in the distant future these men will maintain their status of a civilian corps. The workings of the income tax in Great Britain are different from what they are here. I cannot answer that part of my hon. friend's question.

There would be this distinction and difference: the Canadian fire fighters who go over are sent overseas. The national service in Britain would be at home. Because of that I fancy our men would have a greater moral claim to exemption from the income tax provisions.
Mr. LaFLECHE: May I express thanks for the support I have received in this matter.

The minister has repeated on a number of occasions during the last few minutes that this is a civilian corps. I would deduce from that that little hope arises for these men getting very much consideration with reference to the matter of income tax. Yet from his own statement one learns that the comptroller of the treasury has been ordered not to collect taxes from these men. It would appear to me there is going to be trouble ahead unless some action is taken to clear up the matter, and clear it up very soon. It would not be a very pleasant thing for these men to be faced with the payment of at least two years' taxes if it is discovered that the Minister of National War Services cannot assist them. Would it not be better to collect the taxes and hold them

War Appropriation-War Services
until the point is decided one way or the other upon an official basis? From the way it is being done now, it looks to me as if there are' going to be breakers ahead.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I hope it will not come to what the hon. member for Camrose has stated. Instructions have not been given. But an understanding had been arrived at with the treasury officials, which took place before the date of the report mentioned by my hon. friend, in which it was tacitly agreed by all concerned that they would await a final decision in this matter. While I have not the figures here, the fact is that -in nearly all cases the amount of income tax is not great. The department will continue to try to find relief for these men.

Do
they live in barracks or are they boarded out?
Mr. LaFLECHE: They live in barracks. They are comfortably put up and, through their own exertions and care, they have a very good table.

Firemen who have gone from Canada to Great Britain will learn something over there about fire-fighting under difficult conditions, and will have experiences which they might not have in Canada. It would seem that when they return they would be even better qualified to put out fires in this country. So that their training over there will have been worth while.
Mr. LaFLECHE: The hon. member is quite right. While there is a certain amount of monotony, owing to their having to wait for the enemy to come, it is not that way all the time. Members of the corps' are continually being sent to training schools in the British isles operated by the national fire service. I am pleased to report that the performance of members of our corps at such schools has been very good indeed. They learn about that which has to do with fighting fires under conditions prevailing in the British isles, taking into consideration incendiary bombs, the possibility of asphyxiating gases, and they have to be, familiar with making rescues at sea. I would expect to see future chiefs of Canadian fire brigades drawn from members of this corps.

What are the hurdles which have prevented the minister's department for more than two years from arriving at a satisfactory solution of this simple problem?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I assure the hon. member it is not a simple problem, because it might run into many spheres of the civilian side of
war activities. A favourable decision would have to come from the Minister of National Revenue. But he cannot make his recommendation offhand, since he must take many factors into consideration. For instance, the relief recently given to supervisors of auxiliary services was under consideration for a very considerable time.

Too long.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Perhaps. But due care and attention must be paid when something of that kind is undertaken. The action taken is hardly ever limited to the particular field one may have under survey at the moment.

Item agreed to.
Committee on cooperation in Canadian citizenship, $46,367.

I have two or three questions to ask. First I would ask for a detailed account of the item.
Mr. LaFLECHE: That section of the Department of National War Services known as the committee on cooperation in Canadian citizenship had approved for it last year a total of $18,347, while this year the amount asked for is $46,367. The estimate is made up
as follows:
Salaries	 $33,892
Cost of living bonus	 1.100
Unemployment insurance	 75
Travelling expenses	 10,000
Printing and stationery	 300
Miscellaneous	 1,000
It may be known to only a few that this section has suffered in a. most noteworthy manner, in fact has suffered as no other organization of which I have known, from the crippling effects of illness and indisposition among the small membership of the staff. Each member of the staff has at one time or another been off work with what was certified to by a doctor as an ailment sufficient to put the employee on the shelf for the time being. The aims and objects of the branch are very high. They have to do with helping newcomers to Canadian citizenship to become better Canadian citizens. The aim is somewhat idealistic, but I have always felt that there is a definite place for it, and that people who come to live here should be assisted as much as possible.
I am certain it is not known that the recommendation was made to me, as minister, that this branch be done away with. I kept it on-nursed it, if you like-because I have always felt that we have to have some such organization. The past work of the branch has run pretty much on a level until recently.

War Appropriation-War Services
It has always done about the same thing; in fact, I do not think a graph would show much deviation.
Recently, however, it has been possible to obtain the services of a gentleman who, in my opinion and that of others, is highly qualified. I believe he will be able to lift up this work to that high level I believe it should occupy. I refer to Doctor Robert England, who has accepted a civil service certificate appointment to come to Ottawa to do this work. He will stay here for a few months, during which time I am sure that, not only will this branch show renewed strength, but its work will develop and become greater. So that we may have the extra staff required, I ask for an increase of $24,280 in the salaries item.

What does it actually do?
Mr. LaFLECHE: It keeps in touch with groups of what are known as new Canadians. These are people who come from other lands to settle in Canada. My hon. friend knows there are many such persons. They are to be found everywhere. An attempt is being made to make these people feel at home.

How is the work carried out?
Mr. LaFLECHE: By personal contact at meetings of these persons, and by keeping in touch with the editors of what are known as the foreign language newspapers. Different matters touching on Canadian citizenship are brought to the attention of these people wherever possible through their own publications.
Might we have the amounts paid to these employees?

Will the minister also state the number of employees there are this year? Last year there were four.
Mr. LaFLECHE:	Five, with Doctor
England, and we are increasing the staff. Last year Mr. Tracey Phillips received $4',392, and Doctor Kay, a foreign language newswriter, S3,000.

That has been jumped by S500 this year.
Mr. LaFLECHE: On the recommendation of the civil service commission. There was an editorial assistant at $2,400, which is an increase. There was a stenographer at $1,200. Those are the four for last year. For this year there is a director at $4,500; one research assistant at $3,600; a liaison officer with the foreign language press, $3,000; a liaison officer

with the English and French press, $3,000; one editor at $2,800; two readers at $1,920, and two stenographers at $1,080.

Are the present personnel being retained?
Mr. LaFLECHE: Yes, and there will be additions this year. As I see the picture, it is necessary to add to the staff. It was recommended that I disband this section, but I could not see my way clear to do so. I think we owe it to these newcomers to carry on this cooperation in this way.

Some hon. members have complained about bureaucracy. Last year this item was $18,000 and this year it is $46,367, almost twice as .much. Time marches on, bureaucracy marches on. Doctor England is employed to teach something that is nonexistent, Canadian citizenship. We have been told that our nation is the equal of any nation in the world, but the fact is that we are just colonials. I have been criticized many times because I told the truth, because I did not want to feed people with words to make them believe that they were more important than they were. We have heard much about the progress that has been achieved by the enactment of the statute of Westminster, but that is just bunk. Mr. Chaloult, provincial member for Lotbiniere, has been arrested because he has expressed his feelings in public. If there are people who are called ultra-nationals in the province of Quebec, it is because some people have given more importance to the statute of Westminster than it deserves.
Over the radio we hear a silly programme called, "Metairie Rancourt". There are imperialists who want to have the union jack as our flag. That is their business, and that is our flag at the present time. Some people are for having a Canadian flag. I think the matter deserves consideration. But the fact is that our national flag is now the union jack, and we are the only country in the British empire without a national flag. We are asked to provide money to promote cooperation in Canadian citizenship. What is this for? Is it to put in the minds of the people who listen to the radio the idea that there is a Canadian flag?
As I say, I listened to a programme over the C.B.C. called, "Metairie Rancourt". I do not know who wrote this nor do I know how much was paid for it. I intend to quote from this programme in English as well as in French so that it may be understood by those who are bilingual as well as by those who are not. I had never heard of this programme before, but it was supposed to be a father

War Appropriation-War Services
talking to his children and telling them, "Nous avons notre drapeau, notre drapeau, c'est le drapeau fleur delise". I have not the proper translation of that, but in effect he was saying that we have a flag, that this is our flag, that this is the old French flag. That was what was going out over the national network. Someone was trying to fool the people who were listening to that programme. I object to that sort of thing most strenuously.
What we should do to have Canadian citizenship is a change in our passports; they should refer to us as Canadian citizens instead of British. But the minister would never dare to suggest that, and there are very few members who would dare to suggest it. Why talk of Canadian citizenship when we are still British citizens? I am not ashamed of being a British subject, but I would be prouder if I were a Canadian subject, if I were respected throughout the world as a Canadian subject. Hon. members should read the speeches made by Mr. Lapointe on two occasions during the first session of 1939. He was referring to citizenship, and he stated that a Canadian was a British citizen in this country as well as in the British isles, which was, according to him, another reason why we should not be neutral [DOT]during the war.
The Minister of National War Services will not increase the importance of his department by increasing the staff of such branches, which should not be there to fool the Canadian people. If someone says that I am against Canadian citizenship, that is untrue. But I want my people to be informed of the facts as they are. Instead of being giants internationally, we are dwarfs, and we are dwarfs just because of an inferiority complex on the part of these people who try to give the Canadian people the impression that they are international giants when they are not. Is that clear enough? And that is done in times of war when it is impossible to get a pension for our boys who! are wounded and for those who are discharged from the army. There will be all these doctors, the pests of the universe, who will come here to bring about "cooperation in Canadian citizenship". It is just a waste of time and money because, when it comes down to facts, nothing is done. It will not take $46,367 to give Canadian [DOT]citizenship to our own people. The only thing to do is for the Prime Minister, now in London, to say to Mr. Churchill: The Canadians want to be called Canadian subjects. And they will remain in the British empire just the same. That will be sufficient to give us Canadian citizenship and that will save $46,367 to the Canadian people.
Moreover, I cannot see why we talk about Canadian citizenship when not long ago Senator Robertson or Robinson-I am not sure of his name but he is the national chairman of the National Liberal Federation-dared to say in public that the Prime Minister would go to London as the leader of the small nations, and when Viscount Cranbome said in London the other day that everything would be decided by the big powers and that the small powers would have to listen to the big powers. How can we speak of Canadian citizenship then? We must tell the truth to the Canadian people, and if the wartime information board is the misinformation board, it is the duty of the members of parliament to inform their constituents and the Canadian people as to the real facts. That is my view, Mr. Chairman, and I cannot conceive that members of parliament will let this item pass.
Cooperation in Canadian citizenship! What is that? The worst thing for national unity is the campaign that is made for it. The Canadian people are under the impression that if somehting is done or is not done, it is to appease one of the provinces. How many are afraid to do the right thing and to tell the people that if conscription has apparently not been passed, it is not to appease the province of Quebec because man-power in that province is at rock-bottom just as it is in the rest of Canada, and that it would destroy the war effort of Canada to impose conscription. But no member of the government has the courage to say to the Canadian people that the man in overalls is doing as much to win the war as the man who carries a rifle. And so it all comes on the back of the province of Quebec. It is to appease the province of Quebec, forsooth, that we have not conscription! Is that not a shame? Why not tell the truth so that the people will understand? I am against the policy of appeasing this one Or that one, of not doing this thing or that thing for fear of displeasing someone. There must be a reason for doing a thing, and why not give the right reason? Then no money will need to be wasted on such an item as this. It is revolting to see how public money is wasted. Cents are economized and dollars are wasted, especially in this department, which I denounce with all the strength I have.
Then there are publications presumably to give out news. Little papers are sent out. It is like the images which supposedly would cure stomach ills if swallowed by a sick person. Probably "Nouvelles Catholiques" are got out to make people forget the distribution of condoms by the department of health-

War Appropriation-War Services
"Nouvelles Catholiques:' on the one hand and condoms on the other. It is sanctimonious. Religion itself is a very good thing and it would be excellent to have chapels for the soldiers in the camps. But those chapels are not built. We should have chapels for spiritual worship. Then "Nouvelles Catho-liques" are published and sent all over, while the young men in the camps very often have no place to worship. Instead of wasting time on these useless branches of the department, the Minister of National War Services, who has had good experience as a former deputy minister of the Department of National Defence, should say something to his colleagues, especially his colleague the Minister of National Defence for Air, to see to it that the bright young men in any branch of the army should have facilities for worship, so that each one can pray to God in his own manner. They must rely on the Divine Providence for help in their undertakings, and they must have the fullest support from the government in that connection. That is one thing.
Next, dispense with all these frills and get back to fundamentals. See that the people of Canada are not deceived by false propaganda. Then I hope that there will be a strong wind to dissipate all the clouds that prevent information from reaching the Canadian people. When one speaks as I do, if he does not commit blasphemy, he may be accused of being sacrilegious when he is throwing down false idols.
The only way to have true Canadian citizenship in this land is first to get rid of an inferiority complex as compared with any outsider. A Canadian, even if he is a British subject, does not have the official right to call himself a Canadian citizen. But first he must have pride in his own country, whether Canada is his native country or his country of adoption. A Canadian must be proud of being a Canadian. That is the first thing.
The second thing is that there should be no false representation to anyone. Then there must be no appeasement of any kind, and by appeasement I mean the abandonment of the rights of some people under the pretext of pleasing some other part of the population. These are most serious matters. When the right thing is done, no one is afraid to call it by its proper name; when the wrong thing is done, everyone is evasive.
Since there has been a denunciation of bureaucracy throughout Canada I hope the protests against this item will be so strong that the Minister of National War Services will cancel the engagement of Doctor England

and all his staff and wait until we are Canadian citizens in fact as well as in name before undertaking any further expenditures of this kind.

I should like to find out something about this famous committee. I believe it is a waste of money to have what appears to be a new item for $46,367 for a committee on cooperation in Canadian citizenship. We have so many committees that the House of Commons has very little control over expenditures. This committee is to consist of four men; soon there will be five, and it will be their job to try to improve the standard of citizenship among newcomers. I am absolutely opposed to this proposal. We had a gentleman named Professor Kirkconnell, who wrote a national war book for the government glorifying those who had been born in Europe, at the expense of the native born, the British born and the French who have been here for so many years. He was-engaged by the predecessor of the present minister. I do not blame the minister for these items, because most of the abuses which have been brought to his attention were there before he took over the department. This is an innovation.
The other day he discussed a charities committee headed by Mr. Charles Burton, who has done splendid work in connection with education, and in many public and private charities, and is a great citizen of Toronto and an outstanding Canadian. That committee includes men like Mr. F. K. Morrow, Mr. Gordon Perry and others, who have worked day and night and have effected large economies in the war charities branch. I have known the chairman of that committee, Mr. Charles Burton, for many years; he is a leading citizen of Toronto, a large employer of labour, who has rendered splendid service to the city, the province, the dominion and the empire. Now we are to have another committee of a different kind altogether appointed, which as I see it will be largely a political committee that will create more disunity than unity in Canada and do nothing but talk.
In the fifth year of the war why should it be necesary to appoint a committee to bring about cooperation in connection with Canadian citizenship? Why are these people admitted to the country unless they know all about citizenship and matters of that kind? This is just catering to a certain element in the country, many of whom have taken no part at all" in our war effort. Some of them are conscientious objectors. We are spending four billion dollars of the money of the taxpayers, and dear knows the time has come for retrenchment and economy. I said this long before the present minister was at the head of this department; I am sorry to have to say it

War Appropriation-War Services
again, because he is not to blame for a great deal of it. I do say this is appealing to sectional interests and will cause widespread disunity. There is no such thing as unity in Canada at the present time, and we might as well admit it. We had some evidence of that this afternoon in regard to the war. Wars are won b3r soldiers, sailors and airmen at the scene of combat. They do not need any committee to teach them cooperation in Canadian citizenship or to tell them what to do. I believe this new item should be struck out;
I do not want to take the government by surprise, but if this were estimates I should like to move that the item be reduced to $1. We must find some method of paring down these estimates, something similar to the system I have already mentioned. Before we know it they will have a hundred on this committee; it will be beyond comparison with the committee of one hundred. When I was head of the Toronto police commission there was a committee of forty and a committee of one hundred; I was asked what the difference was, and I said there were sixty more men on one committee than on the other. One committee looked after the theatres and endeavoured to censor programmes, while the other committee sought to get cooperation in other ways. When my leader was at law school he probabfy saw some of the work of those two famous committees.
This is an absolute waste of money. Where is the committee to' meet; how will it function; how many officials will it have? Is it a military body? I have referred already to one book which was written in connection with cooperation, by Professor Kirkconnell. What has he said? He got up in a lecture at the university of Toronto in January 1942, and said there was no room in Canada for the British-born. In his book for the government he glorified the Japanese, saying there were fewer Japanese than British-born in the law courts. Now he has changed his tune and is writing different pamphlets on communism all the time. I suppose this new committee on cooperation in Canadian citizenship will take university professors who are free in the summer months and have them write another book. Probably the committee will have secretaries, under-secretaries, managers, assistant managers, and so on; they will set up an office here in Ottawa; they will have regional committees all over Canada, and the thing will be ridiculous. I cannot find any such committee in England. This committee is to cooperate in connection with citizenship. What does citizenship mean? It means different things to different people. Some who come here will accept all the
privileges of Canadian citizenship but will do nothing to defend the country in time of war or to aid the government in prosecuting the most disastrous war the world has ever known.
We should cut out a great many of these frills. I predict that next year this item will be for 8100,000, and I think this is a great waste of money. I suppose there will be lectures all over Canada, radio appeals and all that sort of thing. I think it is just a lot of humbug; that word is very often used in the British parliament. You cannot fool the public this way, the taxpayers are getting sick of this sort of thing. All sorts of committees, control boards and so on have been foisted upon parliament, and we have nothing to say about it. I protest; I think the whole thing is becoming farcical; almost every day we are appointing another committee. I move that the item be reduced to SI; that is enough.

I happen to have followed the work of this branch perhaps a little more closely than some hon. members, and I feel that I may be in a position to say something which may throw some light on the subject under discussion. In the first place I wish to congratulate the minister upon having refused to do away with this branch of his department. In my opinion the personnel of this branch should be increased to at least fifty. I am not sure whether many hon. members know there is a similar department in the United States. Too many of us, I think, do not realize that some people who come here from other countries encounter certain special difficulties and problems in which they require assistance and guidance. This branch studies these matters and makes suggestions to various departments of government in regard to these problems.
I know personally some of the men in this branch, and I have had the privilege of appearing with a number of them on platforms addressing various ethnic groups and trying to bring them together in an effort to find a common ground upon which all of us could meet. In the United States there is issued a publication known as "Common Ground", and the title itself suggests the material it contains. This particular publication is devoted entirely to the problems which confront different ethnic groups, and those who contribute to it endeavour to point out to the people of the United States that unless they are ready to find a common ground, unless they do their best to unite on major issues facing their country, they cannot pos-
