sibly be a strong nation which should be united in regard to all matters that demand unity.
To many of us, it seems that there are no special problems of this kind in Canada. Let me say to the committee that in Canada we need not only a branch of a department of this kind to look after this particular work, but an entire department to handle the different groups and to iron out all the difficulties confronting them.
This committee studies the press in foreign languages and records certain valuable information, and if hon. members would care to drop into its office they would be welcome to all the material which they would care to have along the lines I have indicated. I know that had this committee been in existence at the beginning of the war, the government would not have made the blunder it did in putting the ban on all foreign languages with respect to radio broadcasting during the war.
Let us consider some of these groups. They have been exemplary citizens. Their sons are in the armed services and they themselves are doing their best to help Canada win the war. They have always been an ideal type of citizens. But what do we find? At the beginning of the war the government had not the proper information and advice and it refused radio services to any group which did not happen to speak English or French. In my opinion the government has done itself a lot of harm. Surely we should trust our citizens. We should be intelligent enough to be able to use to our advantage the various languages spoken. Why be afraid of them? As I say, the government made a mistake because it did not have the proper advice in these matters. It, therefore, clamped down on so-called foreign broadcasting in Canada. That, in my opinion, was definitely a mistake.
In the United States the government, if I remember correctly, is broadcasting in thirty-six languages. Why not? Why not use every language we know, and do so to our own advantage? It could not harm us at all. It surprises me to find that some hon. members take it for granted that this particular branch of the minister's department is useless, that it is not rendering any useful purpose to Canada. Personally, therefore, having the information which I have about the work of this department, I strongly endorse and support the government in its appropriation of this money for this particular branch and I should like to see the estimate increased and the personnel of the branch extended.
Let us, therefore, tackle properly the problem which we often call the "problem of unity". Well, you can tackle it only by
[Mr. Hlynka.}
studying it, and believe me there are in Canada to-day many problems that could be very well ironed out, resulting in unity.

When I noticed this item under this heading in this department I was at a loss to understand why it should appear there. However, after listening to the speaker who has just taken his seat, it has come to me that in all probability this is only a war measure, so to speak. That really astounds me. If it is so, then I would say that this work has been commenced fifty years too late; it should have been commenced years and years ago. I support the hon. member who has just taken his seat and urge that this work be continued, because I know it has great potentialities, and there is a big field for it.
Just how wisely or well the money has been spent I do not know, but I know the opportunities are there to do a really worthwhile work. I differ with the hon. member for Broadview, who I am sorry is not in his place at the moment, when he says that the item should be reduced to the sum of 81. There is great work to be done in this country. I urge the minister by all means to continue with that work. If I may be permitted I would suggest that not only is that work required among the so-called new Canadians but there is room for that education among other types of Canadians. Some of the things that people take exception to in so far as the new Canadians are concerned go back to the doors of those who in their smug complacency think they are the only ones on God's green earth.
Very often in the past new Canadians have been used when it has suited the advantage of others to do so. When times come along in which they do not need this help the new Canadians were simply no good. That does not tend to Canadian unity. It does not tend to build up Canadian citizenship. I wish to draw this to your attention, Mr. Chairman, and especially to the attention of people who hold that view. Some of us are new Canadians by choice. Many of us are Canadians only by accident of birth. Many of us are new Canadians because we came here prepared to do. our part as citizens of this country. We came here of our own volition appreciating the benefits and the opportunities of this land. We came here preparedto do our part in return for those opportunities. In this country of ours there is room for many, many more people; but we cannot build up Canada, we cannot build up a true Canadian citizenship so long as we have one section pulling here and another section pulling there. We must build upon a found-

ation that anyone is prepared not only to accept the benefits and privileges of citizenship in this country, but to do his part in his community life as well. As citizens of Canada we must give equal opportunity to all who are willing to do their part. [DOT]
In conclusion, may I draw to your attention what I find in many cases to be a sore spot with the so-called new Canadian and in their offspring? May I draw to your attention the system that is followed out in the taking of the census in this country? When the census taker comes around he goes into the homes of these new Canadians and their descendants. He sits down and takes their names. He then asks for the racial origin. Let me give you an example of how it works. I know of a case-and there are many others of a similar nature-where the father was bom in the United States of parents who were born in the United States. The grandparents had come from the little duchy of Luxembourg. Later on, these people came to Canada. This man married a girl who not only was born, raised and educated in Canada but whose children to-day are the seventh generation Canadian-born on the mother's side. When they try to explain that situation to the census taker he writes down the racial origin as German. As I have said, on the mother's side these people were the seventh generation Canadian-born. Even the grandparents on the father's side had never seen the old country, much less Germany, and yet they are entered on the records as of German racial origin. I have nothing to say about any person's racial origin, but that is what happens in this country. You find cases where certain people's children and their children's children are bom and raised in this country and yet we have no Canadian racial origin.
I just leave that with you, Mr. Chairman, and with the hon. members of the committee. I realize that possibly it has nothing to do with the matter that is before us, but it is one part of the many problems that we have to face in this country. Many of th'ose so-called new Canadians are doing their part. I can take you to the constituency I have the honour to represent and show you sons of men who were born in Germany and who to-day are flying over Germany and dropping bombs on it. We have every race, religion and nationality represented in that constituency, and by and large every one of them is trying to do his utmost to be a true Canadian. Tet us forget these differences; let us pull together as Canadians and not one pull gee and the other haw.

Mr. Chairman, I have
only a few words to say. The question is not one of emouraging or discouraging the minister, but rather one of seeing things as they are-and no more than that. I would be the last to oppose any move toward Canadian citizenship, but we cannot have cooperation between things which do not exist. Obviously Canadian citizenship does not now exist, and if it is deemed advisable to have Canadian citizenship we must build it, before attempting any coordination. There are many newcomers in this country; there are many refugees, and every one should have the Canadian spirit. It is not enough to have Canadian citizenship; we must all have the Canadian spirit. What is that spirit? It is love of this country before anything else. Some people do not understand it in that way. One considers that love of this country precludes love for any other country. Some say, "We must have the empire first."
The empire is all right, but the imperialist in Canada is a man without a country. He is a colonial; he thinks first of the motherland. I do not say that in any offensive way, I say it in a realistic way. But we who are not imperialists are also colonials because Canada is just a colony in spite of the pompous designation given to this country. I want to make myself clear about this.
A lot has been said about Canada being autonomous, being the equal of the other countries in the British empire. That is the bunk, that is untrue. Whether imperialists are in the majority or not in this country, the password comes from London as far as they are concerned. Everything said in London impresses them to such an extent that they cannot have a really Canadian spirit. So long as there are imperialists in this country; so long as the imperialists rule this country, it will be impossible to have a Canadian spirit prevail. There may be some people who are imbued with the Canadian spirit, but that is not seen in our legislation. I think it should be easy to discuss this matter without offending anyone.
An imperialist has the right to be an imperialist, just the same as one who is not has the right not to be. It is simply a viewpoint. I shall not surprise the committee by saying that I am not an imperialist. I think of Canada before I think of any country in the British empire or anywhere else. But that does not mean that I am an anti-British. The point of view of some imperialists is to call traitor those who do not share their views. I respect the views of the imperialists even though I do not share them, and I ask

War Appropriation-War Services
for the same treatment. I do not expect them to share my views, at least right away, but I want them to respect my views.
How is it possible for one who is Canadian in spirit to show that he is faithful to his country? It is the simplest thing in the world. In the first place he should have no inferiority complex as far as any other country is concerned. He should consider himself equal to anyone in any other country, not superior but equal. He must not only consider himself so, but act accordingly. Then he must speak the real truth. Why are there difficulties between Canadians at times? It is because the truth is not spoken to all of them. The same gospel is not preached in all the provinces at the same time. There is one kind of thing for one province, and another for another province. Is it any wonder that when people from various parts of the country meet together they are like strangers?
They have not been fed with the same food. The people in Ontario have been told that the people of Quebec are rebels, that they are disloyal to the empire because they do not hold the same views about the British empire being their own country. We may be within the British empire, but we should be Canadians first. This fact is recognized by a large number of Canadians of British origin. Hon. members would be surprised at the number in the armed forces who hold this view. One of the most extraordinary things that has been said is that the French Canadians want to take possession of this country and impose their rule. That is not our point of view at all. All that the French speaking Canadians of Quebec or anywhere else want is to be at peace with their fellow citizens.
They lose no opportunity to help their fellow citizens in the other provinces in times of disaster or catastrophe. Quebec has subscribed very well to *all the victory loans. In this loan the village of Cabano, the birthplace of Major Paul Triquet, V.C., was the first place to reach its quota. If we are to have unity, we must act as we speak; we must tell the truth. We should have nothing to hide from our fellow citizens. There are ambitious people who try to create prejudice in order to make a personal gain, but that is all wrong. My hon. friends may go to Quebec at any time and they will see how well they will be received. Good roads have improved the national unity because they afford an opportunity to people from one part of the country to meet those in another part, to talk to each other and to find out that there is really no difference in their problems. There is no difference between a good Canadian farmer in the province of
Quebec and a good Canadian farmer in the province of Ontario, even though the one may be French speaking and Catholic and the other English speaking and Scotch Presbyterian or English Methodist or a good Irishman. There is no difference at all. The people should meet together and talk things over. We should not have to listen to such false stories as I referred to this afternoon, stories about the French flag being our flag when everyone knows it is not. That was not told in English, it was told in French. It was not sent over a private network, it was sent over the C.B.C.
Why tell lies? Why give people a false impression of other people? That is my view. That is why I object strongly to the statute of Westminster, which is an act of the imperial parliament. That statute was intended to give the dominions or the colonies-I am calling the dominions colonies on purpose-the impression that they were more important than they really are. We hear about the halibut treaty and things like that. We are told that England was not holding Canada by the hand when that treaty was signed. Why was that? We are not autonomous, according to the letter of the law. There are provisions for disallowance in the constitution of Canada, and those sections have never been repealed. But if we pass legislation for two consecutive years it cannot be disallowed by Westminster. I maintain that we shall have no true Canadian citizenship so long as those provisions in the constitution are not repealed. We are not masters of our own destiny, not even to stay within the empire. We are in a state of minority and of guardianship. That is why I cannot listen to anyone who says we are on an equal footing with the other nations of the British empire. That is my point.
To summarize what I have said, I do not want anyone to deceive the Canadian people. I hope that it will be possible to speak to them the plain language of truth, and the country will be so much the better for that.
The minister has said that the aims of this branch are very high. They are to help the newcomers to become better Canadian citizens. What does he mean by that? It is important that the minister explain what he means by good Canadian citizens. He said that it was an idealistic branch and that he had nursed it. I wonder why he cherishes it so much.
Then he said that Doctor Robert England had accepted a civil service appointment. He said that Doctor England had behaved well during the last war and during this war. That I do not deny at all. But once again, because a man has behaved well in a theatre of war

I should like to have full information about Doctor Robert England, where he was born, how long he has been in Canada, and what his qualifications are for the post. I should like to, have the same information with respect to Mr. Tracy Phillips and Doctor Kay, a foreign language newswriter, and the same information with respect to the two editorial assistants. assistant at $3,600; also two liaison officers, one with the foreign language press and the other with the English and French press. These two are the niggers in the woodpile. I am afraid some hon. members who have spoken on this matter, including the hon. member for Temiscouata, are under a misapprehension as to the purpose of this estimate. Last November I was asked to address a rather unique gathering in the city of Winnipeg. A few public-spirited citizens, some of Anglo-Saxon origin and others not of Anglo-Saxon origin, undertook to organize what is known in Winnipeg as the Canada Press club. This club embraces not only representatives of the English language newspapers but also representatives of the twenty foreign language newspapers published in that city. It was the first time these gentlemen had been brought together; some of them had never met the others. Some had brought to Canada from Europe their old ideas, with perhaps some lingering traces of the old racial animosities. The effort that was made was simply to bring them together to promote understanding, to give them a wider view of Canada, its problems, institutions and form of government.
Well, I was asked to address these gentlemen at the initial meeting, and I was profoundly impressed by what happened on that occasion. I endeavoured to explain, I am afraid somewhat inadequately, some of the aspects of Canadian life that were new to many of these people, some of whom had come from Europe only recently or at any rate within recent years. Practically all of those who attended had a word to say. I recall that one was a Sudeten German refugee whom I had the pleasure of admitting to this country in the autumn of 1938. I was greatly impressed by the manifest desire of these gentlemen who were the editors or publishers of these foreign language newspapers to be identified as

These young men were glad of an opportunity to serve their country in the highest form of service that any individual can give.
We have, therefore, no reason to complain of the vote which the Minister of National War Services is presenting to the committee. Those of foreign extraction, if we may use that term, are of all professions in Canada, they are in business in Canada; they are on the farms of Canada; they take their place in rural municipal councils and in our legislatures, and I am very happy to say, and I am sure the committee share the sentiment, that we have in this house a member of the Ukrainian race. I do not altogether agree with his political theories, but I wish to say that he is an acquisition to the house. In the Manitoba legislature, with which I am more familiar, there are seven Ukrainian members, one of whom is the deputy speaker in that legislative body. There is no one who knows the facts who will deny that they are making just as fine and full and useful a contribution to the public business of the country as any other group in our population, and I do not except even those of Anglo-Saxon origin like myself.
The purpose of this vote is simply to broaden the knowledge of the place that our Ukrainians

War Appropriation-War Services
and others as well, Germans, Czechs, Poles, Hungarians, have in the Canadian mosaic of our citizenship. I cannot see why that is not well worth while. I have some personal knowledge of the benefits that have flowed from the work done under this vote, and I would be very sorry indeed if the judgment of the committee was adverse to it.
I am sure it will not be. I am sure there will be general recognition that the vote is serving a very useful purpose.
After all, these Canadians, I care not from what country of continental Europe they came, are making their contribution to our Canadian life. They are making their contribution in agriculture, in the ranks of labour, in our factories, in the professions and in the arts. I believe they have a great contribution to make in what might be termed the aesthetic side of our life, a side often neglected and overlooked. In the arts, and particularly in music, these people have distinguished themselves and have made and are making a splendid contribution to our culture.
I merely wished to make these few remarks in the hope that the committee will agree to the passage of the vote.
I am so delighted with the Minister of Mines and Resources, who is now leading the house, that I will not insist any further on the point.

I agree that we need such a committee because we have in this country people of various nationalities who have to be drawn closer to what we would call the Canadian ideology, people who do their utmost for the war effort. If you go to the steel mills and the aircraft plants, if you go to the factories around Montreal, you will find people who have come from Europe who are producing the weapons of war and who are subscribing money generously to every war loan. They want to do their best for Canada, but it is not very easy for them at times. I have come across Canadians who have come from Europe who, when they had gone to look for a job, were asked what nationality they were. One of them was either Ukrainian or Polish, and somehow or another that fact did not go over very well. They had very great difficulties in procuring employment. I have had people come to me with compensation claims. Everyone of them claimed they could not get the same type of justice as others did. They could not explain themselves very well. They needed somebody to help them.
I would say that the committee as at present constituted is not the best committee that we
should have. We have an advisory committee. That advisory committee is composed of English- and French-speaking Canadians. Why should not there be Canadians of European extraction on the advisory committee, people who have been in this country for a long time? They know something about their people; they know something of their problems. If we must have an advisory committee we should have on it representatives of at least the larger groups of European origin in Canada. There is one man on this advisory committee with whom I want to deal to-night, namely, Watson Kirkconnell. I should say from the start that Professor Watson Kirkconnell cannot make good Canadians. Watson Kirkconnell could advise nobody on how to integrate those people into the war effort. Watson Kirkconnell does not possess the spirit of the united nations. Watson Kirkconnell is at war with the members of the united nations. Those charges may sound drastic. I do not resort to them often, but in a corner store on Sparks street I picked up a little booklet cynically called "Seven Pillars of Freedom". Here are some extracts from that book, and I say to you, Mr. Chairman; that a man who writes this type of material to-day can only do harm to the war effort, to Canadian and united nations unity. He cannot advise anybody on how to be a good Canadian. Speaking about terror, Watson Kirkconnell says the following:
As for the continuing terror, Hitler's concentration camps and party purges have taken at least five million lives (quite apart from the vast destruction of the war); while the Soviet regime, in maintaining its iron rule oyer the Russian people, has done to death in the neighbourhood of twenty-five millions.
Stalin, according to Kirkconnell, is five times as bad as Hitler. This is said by a man who is going to educate the people to be good Canadians and good followers of the united nations:
What is the truth?
We shall discuss that at some other time.
It is true.

I am not surprised at the hon. member making this statement.
Then a little farther on, Watson Kirkconnell makes the following statement:
It is little wonder that the Finns have so long been staging their queer sit-down strike on the frontiers of Russia, since they know all too well the probable results of "unconditional surrender" and the occupation of their country by Soviet troops.
Hitler said the same thing a few weeks ago in an interview with Stockholm correspondents.

What is the hon. member reading from?
IMr. Rose.l

A book entitled "Third Year
of Guerilla," by D. J. Tosevic, with a foreword by Watson Kirkconnell. Again I say that it is impossible for a man like Kirkconnell who thinks as ne does, not to be partial, not to play with a small group of Ukrainians who happen to fall in line with his ideology', not to play with a small group of Yugoslavs who think as he does. That is not unity. That is unity with small groups, small cliques. I would say that. Watson Kirkconnell must go from that committee. He has no place on it. A book like the one I mentioned, "Seven Pillars of Freedom," should not be tolerated at the present time in this country. What is more, I should think that article 39-A of the defence of Canada regulations is a good article with which to deal with Mr. Watson Kirkconnell.

I do not intend to follow the bon. member who has just spoken. I am sorry to think the hon. member for Temiscouata has an inferiority complex and considers he is still a colonist. I do not think I am colonist. I do not think Canadians are colonists. I think it is all nonsense to talk as if we were colonists. We are not colonists. We are a free and sovereign country. We ought to be proud and should not have that inferiority complex attitude. As long as we have that kind of thinking, as long as we think we are inferior, Canada will never take her place as a great nation in the commonwealth of nations. I visualize Canada not as a nation of 11,500,000 people, but as a nation of 25,000,000 to 50,000,000 some time. We shall never get there if we continue thinking with an inferiority complex. We all know that we rule ourselves, that we make our own laws and can do just as we like. What is the use of talking such nonsense?
We want to think about the British empire and the British commonwealth of nations, not of the mistakes which have been made but of the great things that the empire has done. It has been the greatest force for freedom the world has ever known, the greatest force for liberty, the greatest force for the institution of self-government, the greatest force for freedom of speech, as illustrated in our parliament, and as we have just heard.
I am in favour of setting up this board and, provided it operates in the right way, I believe a great deal of good work can be done. New Canadians want to be Canadians. I have known many of them, and I know of the good work being done by those men from various European countries. As a matter of fact, the forbears of many' of our people came from the British isles. Some of my forbears came

War Appropriation-War Services
from Scotland, and others from England. People who come from the British isles may be called new Canadians. When they come here they are Canadians, I do not care what anybody says.	,
Difficulties in connection with racial prejudices and religious prejudices must be ironed out. If we are to have unity in Canada we must do something to iron out those prejudices. Let us keep our traditions; let us remember the past; but for goodness sake do not let us always be harping on the mistakes made hundreds of years ago. Let us think of Canada as a Canada in the great British empire; let us remember what that empire has stood for in days past.
To do its best work for Canada this board must work in cooperation with the educational institutions of our country. It can do much in guiding the work of our schools. Whether we have national unity or do not have it depends upon the work of those schools more than upon what is done by this board. It depends upon what our schools are going to teach our people, and upon whether they are going to teach the best and not the worst of our history', the best of the history of Scotland and the best of the history of Canada. But do not let us have any inferiority complex; do not let us always harp back to some grievances which took place many, many years ago. If we do that we shall never have national unity.
Let us think of Canada as a country of great possibilities; let us think of it as a country in which fine citizens of the future may be made, the same kind of citizens who in the past carved their livings from the woods of this country. Let us not forever have an inferiority complex, expecting the government to do everything for us; rather let us recognize the spirit of free enterprise and democracy. There is lots of room for a great Canada, and that is the way we are going to get it. A board of this kind can be very useful. I have not mentioned one class specifically as being new Canadians, although there are plenty of them. There are Ukrainians, and many other groups. I know what fine citizens they are, and the work they have done in this time of war. Those, like our pioneers, are the people who will help make this country great, and I believe this board can render great service in straightening out the little difficulties and misunderstandings which might arise in our dealings with those new citizens. It could be of great assistance.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words at this time. I was called out of the chamber a few days ago on official
business when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar spent some time in trying to disqualify' Mr. C. L. Burton as a suitable chairman of the war charities committee. In other words, the hon. member thinks Mr. Burton is not competent because of views he expressed in an interview, based upon his experiences when he was compelled to earn his own living at the age of fourteen, and the fact that he could not afford a university education.
May I point out to the hon. member that all education is not necessarily obtained in classrooms; rather, only a very small part of it is obtained there. Some of our most highly educated and cultured men in Canada to-day, of whom Mr. Burton is one, left school in their early years, even as early as the age of fourteen. It is Mr. Burton and men like him who have been responsible for creating the great industries in our country which, with the loyal help of labour, have made possible Canada's great contribution to the winning of the war. But Mr. Burton needs no eulogium from me; his work speaks for itself.
I am afraid this bad habit to whieh I have referred has been spreading of late. When I find that Mr. J. W. McConnell is on this committee I recall that on another occasion the hon. member for Lethbridge made some uncomplimentary and, I thought, entirely unjustified remarks about him. Mr. McConnell, like Mr. Burton, started life as a poor boy. His parents could not give him the advantages of a university education; but because of his natural ability, his great energy and splendid character he attained his present position as one of the great industrial and humanitarian leaders of Canada.
The habit of men like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and others of besmirching the character and integrity of our leading citizens tends to discourage such men from giving public service, and is therefore much to be regretted.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to assure the minister that I support the idea behind the committee now under discussion, provided that committee is really promoting the national unity which we all so much desire. For my own part, I think that in addition to the work of such committees, the best thing we could do to promote national unity and to give people in Canada who come from other countries a sense of being truly Canadian would be to see that they have equal opportunities for education, for employment and for all the other amenities of life in Canada.
I myself was not born a Canadian. Those of us who were bom in other countries must naturally take an interest in the countries

War Appropriation-War Services
sorry to think the minister of this department would share anything with this man Kirkconnell.
I can only say in closing, Mr. Chairman, that any man who does as this man Kirkconnell deliberately does, distort the truth, should suffer as Mr. Churchill says all people should suffer who seek to destroy the unity of the united nations. Speaking in the House of Commons at Westminster, Mr. Churchill once said this of people who try to destroy unity, and I stand by these words:
Whoever by word of mouth or by written statement attempts to destroy the unity of the united nations, it were better for him that a millstone was hung about his neck and he were cast into the sea.
Mr. LaFLECHE: Mr. Chairman, we have heard this evening what I really think is a pity. We have heard one person after another disparaged for something that has no connection with the item before the house. I would much rather listen to a discussion for the development of Canada or for our own edification and happiness. I would much prefer to hear the hon. member for Parkdale speak as he did this evening. We' all know many men who give of their time and their strength and, though not as important, of their money, to work for Canada. They are men of good will, and when I think of those gentlemen, whether it be Mr. Burton, Mr. J. W. McConnell or anybody else, however powerful or however humble, who gives of himself for Canada, particularly at this stage of , the world war, I cannot help being reminded of what the angels sang, when our Saviour was born: "Peace on earth to men of good will". There are many men of good will. Let us honour them.

The setting up of this committee has given rise to quite a number of speeches this afternoon and evening, and as I listened to them I could not help coming to the conclusion that this subject is of great interest to each and every member of the house. The hon. member for Vegreville spoke particularly well. During his speech he asked why people like him who were born in European countries and came to Canada should be called new Canadians. As one who was born, not in this country, but in Scotland and came to Canada in 1909, if I give to him and to the house the viewpoint I had before coming here, it will perhaps answer his question why those from European countries who come here are looked upon as new Canadians rather than those of us who come from England. Ireland or Scotland.
When I left Scotland in 1909 to come to this country I felt that I was coming to a part of my own country because, whether we

like it or not, the fact remains that Great Britain had at one time conquered this country and at the time I came here Canada was looked upon as a colony of Great Britain. It vras a British country, so that when I came here as an immigrant in 1909 I felt that I was coming to a part of my own country where the language I spoke and the life I had led in Scotland would be understood and find a ready response. When I say, Mr. Chairman, that I knew the language or tongue I spoke would be understood in Canada, it may interest the house to know that I have at various times been called a foreigner, and when I first came to the House of Commons it was said that I spoke neither of the two official languages here. But I would have you bear this in mind, that nevertheless I was always able to make myself distinctly understood, and when I read my remarks in Hansard I am sure they compared favourably even with those of members who had won a Rhodes scholarship in Canada. So that I have no apologies to offer in that respect. I well remember the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and myself going before a committee of this house to oppose a certain group from the province of British Columbia. We went before that committee to oppose the Japanese delegation who also appeared before it; and I remember that the reporter in Ottawa for the C.C.F. newspaper wrote what I thought was a rather cheap criticism of our attempt to do some good, when he referred to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and myself as two foreigners who were more or less on a par with the Japanese. However, the Scottish people always have been of a very forgiving nature and we just let that remark slide.
With regard to this committee and the work it will have to do in Canada, it seems to me that very often the emphasis is placed upon what Canadians should do for the various groups in this country. During the years I have been in this country I have come to the conclusion that perhaps we should ask the groups who come here to do something for themselves. It may -well be that we are suspicious of them, that we are somewhat jealous of them and perhaps do not welcome them into the community as cordially as we should. I for one, however, do not see how we can ever become a united country, and a great nation if we allow certain groups within the country to live off by themselves, speak their own language and practically carry on as they did in the country they left. Something has been said recently about Russia and the communists. I am not going to enter into a discussion of those matters to-night, but I have heard a great deal of talk by people who have come from Europe and who belong to the

ITm- Appropriation-TFar Services
communist organization, on the subject of what a great country is Russia. I well remember that during the unemployment years from 1930 to 1938, when people were on relief, I found upon investigation that not one of these Europeans was willing to return to Russia or any other European country, but I learned that some 60,000 people had made application to be returned from Canada to Great Britain, and I say that with a great deal of pride. There must have been something worth while in the British isles when 60,000 people in this country would request that they be returned there during those trying years, while none of those who were condemning the country, the government, the system and everything else, requested that they be sent back to the land of their forefathers.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say in future we shall have to be more careful than we were in the past in admitting people into this country; and I do not say that from any wish to put up the bars against immigration. In the past, however, we have permitted to enter this country certain races who can never become really true Canadians. There is the question of blood. I do not see how you can ever mix Asiatic blood and our blood and make a better race. We must face these facts. We had nothing to do with making the black man, the red man or the white man, but the facts are there; and from my reading I have come to the conclusion that wherever the experiment of mixing oriental and white blood has been tried, the resulting progeny has not contributed to the uplift of the race but rather has been a retrogression. So that I say that in future we shall have to give more careful consideration to the kind of people we permit to enter our country for permanent residence.
Then there are the classes or groups of people who have come to Canada and successfully defied our laws. I do not know how this problem can be met. We have in British Columbia a group known as the Doukhobors, who were brought here under order in council. We in British Columbia seem to be alone in our troubles in that regard; at least no other province has the same problem to face. These people do things which are contrary to our laws; they do things we believe to be disgraceful, but notning has been done to make them obey the law. If any group from the British isles, a group of Scotsmen or Englishmen or Irishmen, had undertaken to disobey the laws of this country, strong measures would have been taken to make them obey; and no matter what it cost I would see to it that every citizen of this country obeys our laws. Until we face actual facts and make up our minds that this must be done, I believe we shall always have trouble. I do not think the fault is
altogether ours. These people are living their own lives, speaking their own language and going their own way. They are doing well, far better than, they would have done in Russia. They are living much happier lives than they would live in the country they came from; at least that is what I have- been told by those to whom I have spoken; yet they are not willing to obey the laws of Canada. This is one of our great problems. If this committee can solve it they will receive all the encouragement and support I can give. This problem has faced every government in the past, however, and is likely to face our governments in the future unless something quite different is done.
I rose particularly to mention these groups within our country and to say to the Minister of National War Services and the Minister of Mines and Resources that those who wish to come to this country after the war will have to be more closely scanned. I for one would not permit any large number of people to take up permanent residence in this country if they could not be assimilated. From some quarters we have heard criticism of the Jews. I do not suppose any country on earth has treated these people better than they have been treated in the British isles, where they look upon those of other racial origins in a different way. We are a little jealous of the business acumen of the Jews; we back away from them, but the Jews who have gone to Great Britain have spurred the British people on to greater efforts in the way of business, and they have been accepted in that country as in no othet country on earth. I think we can learn a great deal from the British method of handling these people, notwithstanding Lord Vansittart's statement that the British have been the most foolish of alt nations in the handling of foreigners.
A little later in the session I intend to deal with the oriental question, but this is all I have to say at the moment.

In view of certain statements made during the debate this afternoon, I should like to say just a word in support of this item for cooperation in Canadian citizenship. I was greatly impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for Vegreville this afternoon, the only person of Ukrainian nationality in this House of Commons, and a very worthy member who on many occasions has contributed greatly to the debates of this house. In the province of Manitoba from which I come, some seven members of the legislative assembly are of the same racial origin, and on various occasions these members have made worth-while contributions not only to the debates of that chamber but in various

War Appropriation-War Services
other ways. In the prairie provinces we have many citizens of various racial origins, and I have been surprised at the extent to which they favour an all-out war effort, giving a lead in this respect to many of our citizens who were born in this country. We may well be proud of these people.
For some years I have been concerned over the lack of pride in Canadian citizenship exhibited in certain sections of Canada. This, I believe, has been due principally to lack of leadership in certain high quarters of this country during the past generation. I cannot help thinking that. One probably should not make comparisons, but that great cosmopolitan nation of various racial origins, the United States of America to the south of us, does exhibit far greater pride in national citizenship in its country than we find throughout the Dominion of Canada. For some reason or another that is the fact, and I think we should try to find out just what that reason is and do something to foster greater unity of pride in the citizenship of Canadians. I believe that all our people should unite in a much greater feeling of pride in Canadian citizenship and in all the worth-while successes of this nation. As was pointed out this afternoon, I think something should be done, in the taking of the census in Canada, whereby persons born in this country might be regarded as Canadians rather than as entirely of the racial origin of their father's side of the house. I am sure this would add greatly to pride of citizenship on the part of people of different racial origins. There should be an amendment in this direction.
I suggest also that there should be some amalgamation of the various services which are split up at present under four departments. We have under the Department of National War Services this item that we are now considering for cooperation in Canadian citizenship. This is something that appears as well in the civil estimates. We have in the Department of Mines and Resources the matter of immigration to Canada. Then we have under the Secretary of State the matter of naturalization, while we have under the Department of Trade and Commerce the taking of the census once in so many years. It seems to me that sound business suggests that these four matters should be consolidated under one department which might be designated the nationality branch.
I am one of those who think that in a country such as Canada, with our vast undeveloped natural resources, our very cheap electrical power and the possibilities for the development of cheap electrical power, we

might well expect, during the generation following the cessation of the present war, a population of from thirty to fifty millions. That being so, it means that we shall have to have far greater immigration on a selective basis, which is a matter that the authorities must take into account and to which they must give a great deal of thought.
I simply want to add this word in support of the vote before us. I do not think the vote for the work that is being done in this regard is enough. In the public accounts, if I may be allowed to refer to them, there is an item of expenditure for the year ended March, 1943, for a gentleman named Simpson, who comes from Saskatchewan, and who has done splendid work in cooperation in Canadian citizenship. I am informed that though these people have been doing great work during the past year, there has been a cessation or a let-up in their activities. That should not have been permitted, and I should like to have an explanation from the minister. I think he should let us know why there has been a let-up.
In my opinion this vote is well worth while. Indeed, I think there should be a great deal more work in this connection. I simply want to add my word in favour of the work that is being done in this regard. Many of these people do not like to be called new Canadians. Many of them are younger people who were born in the country and they make splendid citizens. I think we should have a greater mixing of racial origins throughout the country. We should put ourselves out to bring about a greater assimilation in various districts throughout Canada. I would appreciate it if the minister would explain the let-up in the work in the past year.
In conclusion, may I express, on my own behalf and, I believe, on behalf of my colleagues, our appreciation of the work that is being done, and urge that it be augmented.
Mr. LaFLECHE: There was less of a let-up than is supposed, in that it did not grow as I had desired. This afternoon I explained how this particular brandh, in an extraordinary manner, had been held up by the sickness of the members of the small staff. There were other reasons why it did not grow faster. There was the difficulty of getting proper staff, the difficulty of getting a man to head the branch such as we have now. The increased vote is the measure of the importance I attach to the matter, taking into consideration that one cannot overnight increase the branch several times over with any degree of efficiency. One cannot grow too fast.
