At the outset, Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure you that I am very much in favour of the vote and I regret that it is not a good deal larger, because it is time that some work was started along this line. May I give you my observations. I am one of the new Canadians. I came here before Tom Reid and Ian Mackenzie, but I am still a new Canadian. When I left my own country to settle elsewhere I read about Canada, about its resources and possibilities, and I read that there was room for everyone who was anxious to work. I came to Canada and was told that Canada was a nation composed of two nationalities that were working together, the French Canadian and the Anglo-Saxon. I came to this country forty-four years ago; I have lived here since that time, and I still find that Canada is trying to build up a united nation, while having, not two nationalities but, so to Speak, three; because we have approximately 5,000,000 Anglo-Saxons, approximately 3,000,000 French Canadians, and approximately 2,000,000 so-called foreigners. Consequently, we have to reconcile, both outside this house and inside as well, French Canadians, British Canadians and so-called foreigners.
How are we to make a united nation out of this mixture? It is forty-four years since I came here and I find that we are still struggling to bring about unity. In the country to the south of us do you ever hear of anybody being a Swede or a Frenchman or a Scotsman? No; they are all Americans. When the minister is setting up a committee to study this matter he is doing something which is at least one-third of a century behind the times. If we are to have a united nation in Canada we have to forget the various nationalities I have mentioned.
When I first came here there were many Europeans in the country, most of them good people. They came to Canada hoping to find unity, but what did they do? They went to the United States. Many good native Canadians did the same. Now the United States is filled up and is not asking for more immigrants, whereas we are asking for immigrants, and we need immigrants to develop our resources, which are second to none in the world. As long as we squabble among ourselves, however, French Canadians, British Canadians and foreigners, we shall never get anywhere. If this committee that is set up to study this question can do something we shall be accomplishing a great deal to help unite our country and make a nation out of it. I do not intend to take up any more time, but I give that as my observation in 100-152
support of this committee and this vote. It is a vote that should have been presented to the house at least one-third of a century ago.

As I have listened to this debate I have learned much. Of course I have been in this country longer than the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I came to Canada from the land of the green isle. I came here because I felt it was the best place on earth to which to come and I have never changed my mind. I have not very much patience with any man who leaves a country and then talks about the great things there were in the country he left behind. If he is any good he will bring some of those things with him.
As I listened to the debate I thought of the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he was addressing the youth of Canada and giving them some advice. He said:
You will be face to face with race prejudice, religious prejudice, class prejudice and nationality prejudice. But I would advise you to understand that love is stronger than hate and faith is stronger than doubt.
When I think of the tie that binds us to the old land-and by the old land I mean England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales-I think the 'tie is the affection of a mother. You cannot break it. What is the tie that connects ' us with the country to the south of us? It is the tie of another member of the same family. A neighbour is not strong enough, and we have to be careful to treat both as they ought to be treated. When I hear people speak of their nationality I ask myself, What good are they? What can they do for their country? What can they produce for Canada? What are they thinking about and what is their character worth? I remember when a great artist was asked to paint a picture in support of the text where Christ said:
Suffer the little children to come unto Me.
When the canvas was removed, those children were not all white; they were not all black; they were not all red; they were the children of all nationalities. I remember when I came by the Canadian Pacific railway in 1894. I was expecting great things from my first view of Canada. I was convinced when coming along the Canadian Pacific railway, I looked at the rocks, that this was a rocky country. When I came to Winnipeg and heard the different expressions of speech, heard men saying, "You bet"; "that makes me mad"; "that makes me crazy," I wondered what use Canada was making of the English language. But, of course, you may not agree that I come from that green isle in which is spoken the best English the world over. When I heard



War Appropriation-War Services
a Scotsman use the Scotch accent I used to sit back and wonder how he was able to do it, but he could with comfort, as shown by the hon. minister for New Westminster.
I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster when he says that when we came to Canada we came not only because she spoke the same language but because there were the same sentiments, the same branches of the Christian church to which we could send our children if we were so blessed. When we think of Canada to-day we should be proud of the fact that she is not all British, not all French, and that she does not belong to any other nationality in the world, but that we are a mixture. Look at our position to-day. Over yonder in the west is Russia; to the east is Great Britain; to the south the United States and Canada" in the centre is the heart and soul of the world to-day. There never was a nation that had such opportunities as we have. We have to keep the right things first. I have never considered the right thing to be the dollar yardstick. Leave God out of your nationality. Worship Him as you will but do not leave Him out, and then the peoples who come to this country will get a taste of something which will give them heart to go on.
What about those young Canadians who fall in love with English girls? There have been about three thousand of them. What is to be our reception of them? Are we to tell those little lassies, those young wives and their little ones, when they come, that we love them too; that we are going to see that they get fair play, and that we shall allow them to develop Canada in a way which will beat anything that they have ever seen in the old country? This is a live question and I support this vote wholeheartedly. Let us be men; let us forget narrowness of religious and class bigotry. Let us keep the Almighty first, and then, according to His own statement, all other things shall arrange themselves in rightful order.

I just wish to add a few words to what I have said this afternoon. In the first place I believe I should not allow the remarks of the hon, member for North Battle-ford and the hon. member for Cartier to pass unchallenged. I refer to the remarks which they directed against Professor Kirkconnell. Professor Kirkconnell is not in this committee to defend himself. The very booklet which the hon. member for Cartier and the hon. member for North Battleford quoted contains the following words on its first page:
To my four children for whose sake I covet a democratic and Christian Canada.

In his preface Professor Kirkconnell has this to say. When he undertook to write this booklet and others of similar nature he states that he chose the subject:
For or against Canada?
He then, goes on to state:
On that score, the communists were found guilty of treasonous activity against our country at war, their organization was banned, and many of their leaders were interned. After the Soviets had been attacked by Germany in 1941, our communists professed that the war had now become a holy one-
I believe that Professor Kirkconnell can speak for himself, but he has not the opportunity to answer the remarks which have been directed against him to-night. The hon. member for North Battleford said that she hated to call him "professor" because he degraded the very word. I feel that the hon. member of this committee using such extreme and vitriolic language is really casting a reflection upon herself. It is always the best policy to criticize others, if we choose to, but at the same time reserve our tempers to ourselves. So I say the hon. member for North Battleford, who has been in the house as long as I have, could have chosen her words a little more carefully when speaking of a man who is a fourth generation Canadian and who has written in the neighbourhood of thirty books.
This is what appears on the inside of the cover of the little booklet which was quoted:
Watson Kirkconnell, the author of this volume, is a Scotch-Canadian of the fourth generation, born in 1895 in Port Hope, Ontario. He was educated at Queen's university, Kingston, and at Oxford university; and is now Professor of English in McMaster university, Hamilton. He is the author of some thirty .published works, more than half of them written in the interests of inter-racial understanding, and was awarded in 1942 the Lome Pierce Gold Medal of the Royal Society of Canada "for distinguished contributions to Canadian literature."
- During eighteen years in western Canada, he acquired by close study a unique familiarity with the languages, the press and the political affiliations of the Canadians of European ancestry.
And this is what is found on the back cover:
Professor Kirkconnell has profound admiration and gratitude for the military prowess of our Soviet allies. He insists, however, that we are being flooded with -false propaganda regarding the Soviet Union's economic and political system, and that the exploitation of Russia's war record by our Leftists is part of a revolutionary offensive that has been actually intensified since the dissolution of the Comintern.
That is all I wish to quote from the book.
In addition to that, I should like to quote from a pamphlet written by Professor Kirk-

War Appropriation-War Services
council in which he gives us information about a similar branch in the United States. He says:
The most important single body set up was the foreign nationality branch of the ofhce of strategic services. This branch has a paid staff of forty, under a director with long foreign service in east-central Europe. There are also some sixty voluntary consultants in the universities of the armed services.
In Canada, when this pamphlet was written, there were only four on the paid staff.
Professor Kirkconnell sets out four reasons for the organization of this branch. He states that some of the methods used have been as follows:
(1)	Discrimination against these groups in Canadian industry has been combatted toy the initiation of directives to employers throughout Canada and by constant field work toy Doctor Philipps.
(2)	A major task was the mobilization of European-Canadian communities behind the war effort. This must not toe misunderstood. There was no desire to call new "nationality organizations" into existence. The aim was rather to call for a truce on the old political quarrels and hatreds that so often split up these groups into warring factions, and to associate them rather in a single "holding committee" pledged to the support of Canada at war. All this called for the greatest patience and diplomacy. Sometimes the political fires that were thought to be banked down for the duration showed signs of flaring up. But on the whole, there has been a striking development of conscious "Canadian thinking ' in the communities that have been thus coordinated.
(3)	There has been continual close cooperation with the armed services on the subject of recruiting. In order to encourage this by a recognition of equal rights, steps were taken to have eminent war services toy members of New Canadian groups brought to newspaper notice, to have chaplains of their churches appointed to the forces, and to select promising young soldiers of their groups to training as Canadian officers.
(4)	The foreign language press is being supplied with a regular mimeographed service of war news and articles from a Canadian point of view. A typical contribution, with a view to encouraging a Canadian consciousness based on knowledge, has been a series of biographies of prominent Canadians, including Sir Frederick Banting, Vihjalmur Stefansson, Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and J. S. Plaskett. This material is being supplied by the Writers' War Committee of Canada

Under the chairmanship of Professor Kirkconnell.
One last word. I am not sure whether Professor Kirkconnell gets any remuneration for what he is doing in connection with this committee; but I am sure that it takes hours of his time daily, and I know he is best qualified for the job. He is the only man in Canada who commands over forty languages. He has an opportunity to read newspapers 100-152J
and appear at different functions organized by various groups. Undoubtedly he is in a position to know whether he should or should not make certain recommendations to this branch. He acts in an advisory capacity. I may say, too, that no one man could swing the entire branch his way, if there were not enough grounds for his views.
I wish to reiterate what I said previously, that Professor Kirkconnell in these trying years, when it is pretty difficult for some Canadians to know and understand the mental attitude of each and every group within our boundaries, has given much valuable service to Canada. What has been said has shown that sometimes, instead of receiving credit for public service rendered to the people, one receives blame. Evil is thought of him because he does not happen to suit the wishes of one or another group. Instead of that, I should like to see manifested in Canada a spirit whereby we would be ready to give credit to anyone who has done his best in these times to help Canada. I do not think Professor Kirkconnell deserves the remarks which have been levelled against him to-night.

Mr. Chairman, it has been
refreshing to me to hear the hon. member for Vegreville come to the defence of Professor Kirkconnell, who is a personal acquaintance of mine. The hon. member has done credit to himself by the gracious attitude he has taken toward this distinguished gentleman. At a time like this when we should be attempting to develop national unity it is unfortunate that the hon. member for North Ba'tleford and the hon. member for Cartier should see fit to refer to this distinguished gentleman in the way they did simply because he happened to write something which did not agree with their own political philosophy. We must adopt a different attitude if we are to have national unity in a country like this where there are so many nationalities.
I am one generation removed from the old country. My grandfather brought my father over to this country from Scotland. My people had the blessing of poverty. I am told that my grandfather's income was $25 a year; yet he raised a family of eight children, educated some of them, and landed in Canada in 1852 with approximately $800. I cannot boast of having been born outside Canada, but I am proud of the type of people my ancestors were and that they had courage enough to come to this land in order to create greater opportunities for me.
We cannot expect to hold this great expanse of country on the northern part of this continent with but 12,000,000 people. I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster, who

War Appropriation

War Services
said that when we bring people into this country it is not only to our own interests but to theirs as well that there should be a reasonable amount of selection. We should try to be sure that they will assimilate Canadian ideals.
I regret that anti-Canadian feelings should be expressed within the walls of this building. I believe that if in the past our immigration authorities had showed more care in selecting those who were permitted to come to Canada it would have been better for all of us. If these people have not been able to accept Canadian ideals, they must be very unhappy. They are not contributing anything to Canadian citizenship by advocating their particular philosophy of life. While I have always believed in a selective system of immigration, I have also believed that we should try to maintain a certain standard of Canadian citizenship. People who desire to come to this country should be subject to the scrutiny of our immigration officers. An attempt should be made to see that they are ready to accept the blessings of this country, accept our ideals. If they are not ready to do that, they should get out of the country.
I rose for the purpose of defending Professor Kirkconnell because of the vilification he had been subjected to to-night. I was proud to follow the hon. member for Vegreville. As he has said, he is one of our new Canadians, a Ukrainian, and he has exhibited a high degree of Canadian idealism even though we may not all agree with his particular political philosophy. He has shown the spirit of toleration which is the only thing that will make Canada a great country.

I should like to take part in this debate for a few minutes. Along with other hon. members, I am glad to see this vote in the estimates and I think it would be better if it were a larger vote than it is. I am in agreement with several hon. members who have spoken, because I believe the work of a committee such as this can create tolerance in this country. Tolerance is necessary in Canada and also it is badly needed. Tolerance leads to harmony and there can be no progress in a country without harmony or a reasonable approach to it.
Two hon. members who represent a small minority in this country have spoken tonight, the hon. member for North Battleford and the hon. member for Cartier. In words they advocate tolerance; yet they have given a very poor exhibition of that quality. The hon. member for Vegreville referred correctly to the addresses as being vitriolic. For my part I could not help thinking that the spirit of tolerance shown by these two members

was like the quality exhibited by a certain Irishman. A shoemaker who wanted to set up a business was on the road on the way to Antrim, when he met an Irishman. He inquired about the characteristics of the people in that city, the division as between Protestants and Catholics and so on. The man replied that he would find them pretty well divided, and he added that he got along pretty well with both sections. The shoemaker asked him how he did it and he said it was because of his tolerance. But when he described his tolerance it was somewhat of the quality exhibited to-night by these two members. He said, "On the 17th of March I wear an orange ribbon and on the 12th of July I wear a green shamrock, and if anyone asks me where I hang my hat of a Sunday, I tell him to go to hell and punch him on the jaw."
As I listened to the attack by these two hon. members upon an outstanding Canadian citizen I could not help thinking they have no understanding whatever of the quality which they would like to see current in this country. I do not think there should be any multiplication of words on my part in supporting what has been said by the hon. member for Vegreville and the hon. member for Brant. Professor Kirkconnell was for a long time a citizen of my city and one of our most honoured citizens. The people of my city are a discriminating people, and the fact that Professor Kirkconnell was a particularly honoured citizen of Winnipeg is itself a passport that will carry him anywhere in this country or in any other country.
I had the honour of knowing him slightly, not nearly as well as I should have desired. From all that I have known about him I regret that I was not personally better acquainted with him. My chief reason for rising is that I did have some slight acquaintance with him and I have been able to watch his work over a number of years. He came from my city, and for me to have sat silent when there were ill-tempered outbursts against him would, in my opinion, have been to condone a wrong. I shall say no more than that in characterizing these attacks.
I only hope that the minister will never see fit to deprive himself of the benefit of the advice of that kind of man. If we had many more men like Professor Kirkconnell in this country Canada would be a great deal the richer for it, and I am sure that the few members who have attacked him, when they stop seriously to think this over, will be found to agree with me. The man is doing a great service and has been doing a

War Appropriation-War Services
great service for many years, and it is very cheap stuff to come into this house where he cannot reply and from this safe place be a detractor.

Mr. Chairman, I
should like to support this vote. In view of the fact that the amount asked for by the minister is only twelve and a half dollars for every million dollars we are voting, the hon. member for Broadview is not on very sound ground when he complains of extravagance.
I wish to present a point of view which has so far not been advanced in the debate and suggest that the department should pay some attention to the older Canadians. We have heard a good deal to-night about the new Canadians. Nothing has been said about the responsibility of the department for the old Canadians.
For some fifteen years I have lived in a community in northern Saskatchewan where I have belonged to a minority group. Like the hon. member for Brant, I happen to be of Scottish racial origin and people of Scottish racial origin are in the minority in that community. The 1941 census shows how very cosmopolitan a community Mackenzie is. The largest racial group there is the group to which the hon. member for Vegreville belongs, the Ukrainians. I should like to say, in passing, that I envy the hon. member for Vegreville his ability to speak so fluently in the English language. If the old Canadians would make some effort to become familiar with the language of other peoples-I refer especially to the English-speaking in this country who refuse to become familiar with the French language, and as we know a great many of our old Canadians refuse to make any effort to become familiar with any of the languages spoken by the peoples who come to this country-it would be very much better for us all. The hon. member for Vegreville puts us to shame when he speaks the English language as very few of us are able to speak it.
I was saying that the largest racial group in Mackenzie is Ukrainian, numbering 18,334. The next largest is the Scandinavian group, numbering 8,424; then English, 6,979; Polish, 5,097; Russian, 4,664; Scottish, 4,025; Irish, 3,955. As a member of one of the minority racial groups in that community I wish to say that it has been a great privilege to live with peoples of so many different nationalities who have made a contribution to this country which has been very valuable indeed. So that I hope that the department will not pay too much attention to the suggestions coming from the hon. member for Brant and the hon. member for New Westminster, that at this
stage time should be lost in worrying about whether these people conform to the standards that prevailed in Scotland fifty or sixty or a hundred years ago or conform to the standards which prevail in New Westminster.
I should like to make reference to the valuable contribution which the largest racial group in my community, the Ukrainian group, has made to Canada. They have settled in the northern part of the province where years and years of hard work were required. Many of them went a long distance back from the railway and worked from early morning till late at night, making a great contribution in building up this country. In this time of war, as the Minister of Mines and Resources has said, they have responded in a remarkable way. The man who brings the milk to our home every night is a Ukrainian who has earned his living in a hard way. He has two sons in Italy with the Canadian Army, \ one being a major and the other a lieutenant. The father and mother, so-called new Canadians, have made a valuable contribution to Canadian life.
In some parts of the country criticism is made of our Jewish Canadians. I have a very small number of Jewish citizens in my riding, some 178 persons, but they responded at the earliest moment in the war and have performed distinguished service. Just the other day I received from the headquarters of the Department of National Defence for Air a photograph of Flying Officer Gelmon, from Preeceville, Saskatchewan, who is in service at Ceylon. This young man who is in charge of flying a Catalina observed a ship that had been torpedoed by a Japanese submarine. He landed his flying boat on the water and rescued all the members of that disabled ship's crew. His record was mentioned over the BBC some time ago, and it was not until his parents drew attention to the fact that he suggested it was all part of the day's work. So that I urge that the minister consider increasing this vote and have some regard for the old Canadians and their responsibility, as citizens in a democracy, to their fellow Canadians who do not speak their language.
Just one final word regarding our responsibility to our Chinese Canadians. It is almost a year now since members of this house heard one outstanding woman of the Chinese race, Madame Chiang Kai-shek, address this House of Commons. We were all deeply moved by the message she brought on that occasion and by the leadership she and her distinguished husband have given. We have all been inspired by the contribution which the Chinese people have made in saving democracy for the

War Appropriation-War Services
world. Yet in Canada we refuse to consider the Chinese born in Canada as fellow Canadians should be recognized when we have the four freedoms at stake. Just this week I had occasion to take up with three departments of government the case of a young Chinese Canadian in British Columbia who has been given the run-around in connection with his offer to do his bit in an important public service. We make it very difficult for those who do not fit into the conventional pattern to make their greatest contribution both in war time and peace time. Therefore, I hope the minister will not be unduly influenced by those who have suggested that this vote should be reduced to $1, or who complain about any expenditure of this kind.
In conclusion, I wish to congratulate the minister upon having secured the services of Robert England who, as the minister pointed out, has a distinguished record in the last war and in this war and who during the years has demonstrated that his viewpoint will inspire confidence and good will among the peoples who have come to Canada to make their homes.

I could not permit this debate to conclude without expressing just a word of approval to the minister for having placed this item before us. It seems to me that if there is any criticism of the amount it is that it is too small, not that it is too large. Earlier in this debate various hon. members have been able to speak as newcomers to this country and to tell of their experiences in coming to Canada from some other land, either a part of the empire or a part of Europe. I am not able to express myself along that line, because I am the fourth generation on both sides of my house to call Canada home. I think I am thoroughly acclimatized as a Canadian, and if anyone, other than my French Canadian friends, some of whom have been here for three or four hundred years, has a right to call himself a Canadian, I think I have that right.
With some deference and some humility, I say that it takes time in order to understand Canada and the spirit of Canada. That understanding is not readily acquired. Canada is different from many other countries of the world, because here there is no dominant religion, no dominant race, no dominant nationality other than Canadian. We have been very fortunate in this country in the development of a broad and sympathetic attitude toward others. Tolerance consists for the most part of good manners. Intolerance always expresses itself in unkindness and bad

manners. In our early days we were forced to get along one with the other. I think the French Canadians frequently fail to realize how much in their culture, their diversity of life, their general happiness and well-being they owe to the English-speaking portion of our population. And I can say definitely that we of the English-speaking portion of the Canadian population seldom realize how much we owe to the French. Each owes to the other a .great debt of gratitude, if only for the one thing, that we have been forced to live together and to get along with our neighbours. So that we have developed in this country a constitution and society broad enough to tolerate somebody other than ourselves.
Then, following that experience as between the English and the French, we have had the inestimable value of the introduction into our society of people from other lands, chiefly central Europe. I cannot speak too highly of those people whom we somewhat wrongly call new Canadians. They are not much newer than many of the rest of us, but the term designates them and it will do. I come from a riding which is probably as cosmopolitan as any in Canada, and I have always been proud to claim to be a representative of these various groups. For instance, I have a very large Polish vote, and I am pleased to say that it supported me very generously. My heart bled for these people in 1939 when the German mechanized machine overran their country. We of the English race frequently refer to Great Britain as the motherland, but we fail to realize that Canadians have many motherlands. To a great many Canadians Poland is the mother country, and the Polish people in Canada were sorely hurt when Poland was conquered by Germany. I look forward to the time when I can rejoice with my Polish friends, when once more Poland will be free. On many occasions I have joined in the pledge given to the Polish people by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of this country, that we of the united nations will never sheathe the sword until Poland shall be free. Poland has contributed something to Canada by supplying us with a portion of our population from that bold, fighting race which has struggled for freedom as heroically and as long as any other nation on earth.
I have always been happy to think of myself as a representative of the Ukrainian people of my riding, and I wish to join in the compliments that have been expressed to the hon. member for Vegreville. I was sorry, however,

War Appropriation-War Services
that in his recent speech he discussed personalities. I am not much interested in persons, either in attacking or in defending them, for usually they can look after themselves, and that is particularly so in this instance. It is unfortunate that personalities should have been brought into a debate so lovely as this. We are struggling for unity among these races, and you cannot get unity by bringing up here the divisions that you may find in the old land. That is an unfortunate thing that is happening in Canada. These various groups of our population should divide now upon Canadian questions, not upon European matters. So often I find that various portions of the same racial group hate each other because of imported divisions, not because of Canadian divisions. I have been proud to represent the Ukrainian people, whom I have found to be of sterling good character, industrious, strong, healthy, vigorous both in mind and body; a kindly people, very much like ourselves. I have been proud to represent the Italian people of this country, of whom I have a considerable number in my riding. My heart bled for them when we declared war upon Mussolini and left them in a most unenviable position. They are a kindly people thoroughly Canadian, as has been proved by their actions during this war.
Fortunately I come from a riding in which there is not one dominant religion but which is fairly equally divided as between the Catholic, Protestant and Jewish faiths. I feel sure that if more people enjoyed the advantages I have bad they would recognize the virtues of these different groups, and there would be less anti-Semitism and fewer antagonisms over opinions on religion.
I welcome this vote. I know it is not necessary to defend it, but I do want to express my approval of it and I hope that every dollar will be spent wisely, as I am sure it will, in developing the idea of a Canada different from most countries, as I have said, not of one race, not of one nationality, not of one religion, but rather a collection of groups each with a respect for the rights of the others and each with sufficient good manners to get along with the rest. Let us have in Canada a nationality broad enough to include within the folds of our common flag men of all races, of all religions, of all nationalities, yes, and of all political opinions.
It is not necessary that men who come from other countries should forget the country of their origin. I have always thought and have preached to those various groups that they are doing a favour to Canada when they maintain their ancient traditions and teach
[DOT] $
their children the language of their own country. True, it is necessary that they should learn English because that is the language of the dominant language group. It is the dominant language. They will be handicapped if they do not know English. At the same time, they will lose the culture of their own country unless they teach their children the language of their birth.
It is wise that the Polish Canadian should remember the Polish language, its customs and its glorious history. It is wise that Ukrainian Canadians should remember the history of the Ukraine and rejoice that the foreign invader is being chased out of the Ukraine. It is wise that the sons of the Italian Canadian should know the music, history and literature of Italy, and that his children should carry on that glorious inheritance. Canada has been the gainer by the culture, the language, the knowledge and the diversity that these people have brought to our shores. Canada will be a great nation when finally we unite all of these nationalities and groups into one great united and homogenous people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
There is one note of warning in connection with this vote which I should like to sound, but before I do so I wish to say that I agree with those who feel that the amount is far too small for the purpose to which it is to be devoted. I am sure it is significant that there has been a debate of this length on an item relatively so small. It indicates that the members of this house feel the importance that attaches to any effort to develop the consciousness of Canadian citizenship among all our people and the sense of unity throughout our country. I feel, too, that I should add to what some other hon. members have said by way of commendation in connection with the securing of Robert England to head this work. I was disappointed and a little disturbed some months ago when Mr. England's resignation was announced from a post in another department of the government, and therefore I was pleased to learn that he had been secured for this very important work.
The minister, speaking earlier this evening about Mr. England's qualifications, mentioned a number of points. I am not sure whether he referred to the fact that his interest in this kind of thing is by no means new. I happen to know Mr. England personally and I know that his interest in the matter we are discussing extends over a number of years. In fact, several years ago he produced a very worth-while book on the subject of central

War Appropriation-War Services
European immigrants in Canada, and I am sure he brings to this task not only the kind of interest that one needs to further this sort of work but the knowledge, ability and experience that are also very necessary. I hope, therefore, that the government will be able to secure, in addition to Mr. England, others who will likewise add to the calibre and quality of the work of this branch, and I hope it will be recognized by the government not just as a branch for which money should be voted in a time of war but rather as a phase of work that should be established on a permanent basis.
I said when I rose to my feet that there was one note of warning I should like to sound. I understand that part of the work of this committee is to feed to our foreign language newspapers material which will enable readers of those papers to get the best ideas about the country in which they are now living, and I may say to the minister that certain eom-. plaints have come to me from time to time. I am not sure whether the material that is complained about results from the work of this committee, but it sounds as though it does, from what the minister said earlier to-day. The complaints have been that the material, while it seemed to be boosting Canada and our institutions and form of government, did seem to flavour of propaganda for the government of the day. I sound that note of warning not out of any sense of jealousy. My point is that if anything of that kind does creep in ' it will defeat the very purpose of a vote of this kind, and I hope the minister will see to it that in so far as it is the job of this committee to feed to the foreign language press of the country articles that boost Canada, to sell to our people the glory of Canadian citizenship and of our institutions, he will see to it that this work is kept free from anything that could be labeled as partisan propaganda.
With that note of warning I wish to repeat what I have already said, that I not only support this vote, but commend the minister for having secured the services of Mr. England to head this work, and I hope that the government will see to it that it is established on a permanent basis.

Some remarks have been passed this evening regarding what I said on the matter of Mr. Kirkconnell. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre stated that I was a little intolerant and a little vicious in my remarks, and so on. I am intolerant, toward one thing, fascism, as I would be intolerant toward any foul and evil thing. I am intolerant, too, of those who by their
fMr. ICnowles.]
activities over a period of years have striven to misrepresent to the people of this country fascism and the forces which have fought against it. Although some hon. members of this committee may have personal relationships with Mr. Kirkconnell, that is not the question. It is his work over a period of years, which can be traced very distinctly from his writing, that I am concerned with. The hon. member for Vegreville states that he speaks forty languages. He read out some of the publisher's remarks. That does not say anything to the man's credit at all. Because he speaks forty languages it does not mean to say that he promotes unity. It is a very nice thing for the hon. member for Vegreville to speak about unity and tolerance. You see, the spectacle of the hon. member for Vegreville supporting Mr. Kirkconnell is quite simple to understand. I understand it perfectly. They have had a relationship over a period of years, and it is a case of the two of them being very like-minded. Naturally the hon. member for Vegreville thinks Mr. Kirkconnell is all right. I have in my hand a series of small magazines. They are printed in Ukrainian. The name is "The Call". A series of them have been translated for me. I find in them some of the most vicious and intolerant statements that I have ever found anywhere. Here you will see a gruesome picture and underneath a series of statements, vicious anti-Semitism. The editor is the hon. member for Vegreville. It is very nice for certain people these days to turn around and speak about tolerance. I have no tolerance for fascists and for those who have promoted disunity in the past in this country. I want unity against fascism, and whoever likes to disagree with me let them take their stand. I am against fascism. That is all I wish to say.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I wish to say a few words before the vote carries. As we all know, there are groups of people whom we term new Canadians. They are found nearly everywhere in Canada. I take it from the excellent speeches made this evening that this committee is definitely of the opinion that these new Canadians shall not remain strangers within our gates; that there is a widespread desire, as represented by what has been said in this committee, to do our share to help these men, women and their children to love Canada more because they will know Canada better.
I must say that I am tolerant, although in some respects I find it extremely difficult to be kind even in thought to certain kinds of people. But those who live in Canada, those who during this war have done good work, have my appreciation. I certainly am tolerant

War Appropriation-War Services
toward them, and in saying that I have in mind the gentlemen who have been taken to task this evening altogether too harshly. In my opinion that is the case. I do not know Professor Kirkconnell very well, but from my point of view and my knowledge of the work he does for my department I have every reason to believe he is an excellent gentleman. What other people may think of him I do not know, because I do not know their relationship with him.
At any rate, Mr. Chairman, this has been a very encouraging day to me. Whilst our boys are fighting for our safety we at home should work at national unity. I think this has been a good day in that regard.

I wish to say that in so far as Professor Kirkconnell is concerned I reaffirm what I said this afternoon. He was engaged by this government to write a book to which I objected in this house in 1940 and 1941. The book dealt with the British born and the foreign born. It was the glorification of the foreign born as against the other. From the information contained in the immigration figures at the time I say the information contained in his book was wrong. In this book he said that the British born had more cases in the law courts than the Japanese. I opposed it at the time and called the attention of the committee to the booklet. It was circulated in England and did a lot of harm to immigration. He made a speech at the university of Toronto in January, 1942, in which he said there was no more room in this country for the British born. He said there was no land available. That was after the battle of London. I looked into the book. It was a glorification of one section of the country against the other. He has changed it all now. He seems to be writing books the other way at the present time. He seems to be writing books on communism now. I have expressed no opinion about what he said, but I have been an opponent of that particular system for many years. My views are well known to this committee. I reaffirm and reassert what I said this afternoon. I believe there should be equality of treatment for all classes. I believe there should not be race or religious jealousy in this country. I have never had any and I have not had any at any time in this committee. That is all I wish to say regarding that professor. He goes on to refer to other component races who have been here for generations. I obtained the booklet at the time it was printed. Large numbers of copies 100-153
were distributed in England at a grave time of the war in 1941 and did great damage to immigration from the British isles and from other places.

I wish to take a minute or two to correct the impression which perhaps may have been left by the remarks of the hon. member for North Battleford. It seems that the hon. member is making a habit of attacking certain individuals. She made a statement to the effect that some of my writings which appeared in the publication which I published in 1935 contained writings which were anti-Semitic. I wish to state, here and now, that at no time in my life have I ever written anything or said anything which was anti-Semitic. I wish to add also that just because I was the publisher of the magazine it does not necessarily mean that I wrote every word that appeared on the pages thereof. Certain individuals contributed to my publication and I published the things which I felt would be of interest to my people. One of the writers who came from Europe and who was a witness of conditions there, and who knew the history, wrote an article which condemned certain leading men of Jewish nationality in . the Soviet Union. That was all. Therefore the article was not mine at all. There were two articles altogether on this subject. The other article which appeared was a translation by another man also. He asked me to publish it and I did. I published not only articles that were anti-this or anti-that, but articles that were of various natures, articles which gave information on various topics
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I wish to correct this propaganda which has been circulated and levelled at me personally for many years of being anti-Semitic. I never have been and I never intend to be, because I have not the reason for it, and it is not in my make-up. So I just wish to correct the remarks which the hon. member made to-night.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
Mr. RALSTON moved the adjournment of the house.
What is the business for to-morrow?

As business for to-morrow we propose to continue with the war appropriation resolution, but it is proposed to suspend consideration of the item under the Department of National War Services and take up the items under the Department of Labour.

Business of the House

If that should by any chance be finished, we shall resume with the Department of National War Services.

I wish to lodge a protest to the acting leader of the government with respect to this change in the order of business in connection with the war appropriation resolutions. There was a definite arrangement made both last session and this session that these departments would be taken up, one department after another, and when one department was finished another would be commenced. This is the first time in two sessions that the government has asked for a change in that arrangement, which was entered into at the time at the instance of the government, if I may say so. I wish to protest. I do not know how far my protest will go, because I recognize the government has some powers in these matters. However, we are not in favour of it.
Unless there is some extraordinary circumstance of an emergent nature we do not wish to have the order changed, because this procedure establishes a change not only now, but also establishes a precedent which perhaps might be carried into another session as well. I think our rights must be protected, and for that reason I rise to protest, and ask the government not to make the change which is suggested.

I say to my hon. friend that I would be the last to attempt to break any arrangement which has been made. I am not conscious of any arrangement such as my hon. friend suggests. We do this in connection with other items; that is to say, on the estimates. We take up one department and do not finish it, and another department may come in next. My hon. friend is quite right when he says it has been the custom to continue with one department and go through with it before another is reached, under the war appropriation measure.
However, in this instance, the circumstances happen to be special, and I would hope that my hon. friend would so consider them. They happen to be of a special nature. My colleague the Minister of Labour will have to leave to go back to the conference at Philadelphia very shortly and he is anxious, and I believe the house and country will be as anxious as he is, that the items under his name might be taken up-and I hope finished-before he goes.
In connection with the length of time which has been taken in the discussion by the estimates of the Department of National War Services, I may say, without any criticism whatsoever, that they have been considerably

longer than was anticipated. It is necessary that the committee should at least begin the discussion of the items under the department of the Minister of Labour, because there are one or two other matters of very important business which necessarily will have to be brought in next week. And it may be that if this procedure is not followed the items under his department may not be finished before he goes. That is the special circumstance under which this is being done.
I join with my hon. friend most heartily in the desire to finish one department before another is brought on, because I think that is the easiest way to do business-certainly it is the easiest for the government. Then, members of the cabinet are not kept waiting for their estimates, and they are not so uncertain as to when they may come up. But this is a special case, and 1 trust hon. members, including my hon. friend, will so regard it, having regard to all the circumstances.
How long is the Philadelphia conference supposed to last?

I cannot tell my hon.
friend that.

May I say to the leader of the government that there is no guarantee, as I see it, that the Minister of Labour will be allowed to proceed during the next week to a point where he would finish his war appropriation estimates. That puts it in a very awkward position, so far as we are concerned. I believe we are perhaps going to find ourselves with the estimates of the Department of National War Services unfinished, with those of the Department of Labour unfinished, and with certain new legislation which it is expected will be taken Monday in an unfinished state. That is the position.
For these reasons we protest against the change. As I say, perhaps the government has the right to set the programme, and to make a change in a succeeding session; but I must confess that I am very much disappointed that the government has taken this position. It has upset, and will upset the arrangements which were arrived at and which, I repeat, were not arrangements entered into lightly. They were arrangements which definitely formed part and parcel of the whole war appropriations resolutions debate structure.

I am sorry my hon.
friend has repeated what he said, because I think he will find there was no arrangement that each department would be taken through to the last item. In the second place I sub-

Housing
mit to the house that the circumstances which I have mentioned- are extraordinary and should be taken into consideration. I hope the house will do that.
Third, may I say I do not quite share some of the apprehensions entertained by -my hon. friend with respect to the -fact that there is more than one item of unfinished business before the house. With all due respect, in my fourteen years in the house I have not seen -much evidence of the house going right through with any important item before taking up anything else. The house has been anxious to put its business forward one or two stages at least, and then proceed to the discussion of some other item.
That is what is being done here, and I do not think there is anything very shocking about it. I do trust that the result will show that nothing has been done to interfere with the rights of hon. members, and I hope it will be found that this procedure will expedite public business.
And last, but in my mind not the least, the items standing in the name of the Minister of Labour are extremely important. I have been anxious particularly to see to it that the service departments, and the departments more vitally connected with the war, should be before the house as soon as possible. I hope the house will enter upon the business to-morrow as I have outlined it.

Would the Minister of
Labour be kind enough to say how long that conference is intended to last?
I do not know.
